alias.summary: The POSIX alias utility creates, replaces, and displays shell aliases. Use unalias to remove one alias or all aliases.
alias.explanation: The shell stores an alias as a name and replacement string. When the shell reads that alias name as a command, it substitutes the stored string. The definition belongs to the current shell and its subshells, not to the parent shell or separate utilities. Use unalias to remove one alias or all aliases.
alias.syntax:
alias [ alias-name [ = string ] ... ]
unalias alias-name ...
unalias -a

parameters.name: alias-name
parameters.description: An alias name to display, or the name used on the left side of an assignment.

parameters.name: string
parameters.description: The replacement text stored for the alias.

parameters.name: alias-name
parameters.description: An alias name to remove with unalias.

parameters.name: -a
parameters.description: Remove all aliases when used with unalias.

alias.returns: alias returns 0 on success. It returns a value greater than 0 if a requested alias is missing or an error occurs. unalias returns a value greater than 0 if a named alias is not valid or an error occurs.

example.explanation: This defines a shortcut, uses it, and then removes it.

useCases.scenario: Create a short command for a frequently used command line.

useCases.title: Inspect shell aliases
useCases.scenario: List aliases while checking the current shell setup.

useCases.title: Delete an alias
useCases.scenario: Remove a shortcut that is no longer wanted.

useCases.title: Clear aliases before a script
useCases.scenario: Start a cautious shell script without inherited aliases.

interview.question: What does alias do?
interview.answer: alias creates or replaces an alias in the current shell. The alias name is replaced by its stored string when the shell encounters it as a command name. The definition is also available to subshells.
interview.followUp: How can an alias be inspected? Use command -v name; for an alias, it reports a command line representing the alias definition, although separate utility environments may not identify aliases correctly.

interview.question: How do you create and inspect aliases?
interview.answer: Run alias with no operands to display all aliases. Give one alias name to display that alias. Give name=string to create or redefine it.
interview.followUp: What output format should a script expect from alias? POSIX specifies name=value followed by a newline, with quoting suitable for shell reinput.

interview.question: How are aliases removed?
interview.answer: unalias name removes one named alias. unalias -a removes every alias in the current shell environment. It returns a nonzero status if a named alias is invalid or an error occurs.
interview.followUp: Why might a script use an escaped unalias -a? Escaping prevents an existing alias from changing the unalias command itself.

keyPoints: alias either defines an alias or prints an existing definition.
The POSIX form accepts zero or more definitions or alias names.
With no arguments, alias lists every alias.
Use name=string to create or replace an alias.
unalias changes the current shell environment.
unalias -a removes all aliases.
gotchas: An alias does not change the parent shell. Create it in the shell where you will use it.
Alias output is shell-quoted. Do not assume the displayed text is a plain, unquoted value.

awk.summary: awk scans text records, splits them into fields, and runs actions for records that match program patterns. It supports input files, standard input, variable assignments, and BEGIN and END processing.
awk.explanation: awk reads input as records, usually lines, and splits each record into fields. It checks each record against program patterns and runs the action for every matching pattern. BEGIN actions run before input, and END actions run after all input.
awk.syntax:
awk [ -F sepstring ] [ -v assignment ] ... program [ argument ... ]
awk [ -F sepstring ] -f progfile [ -f progfile ] ... [ -v assignment ] ... [ argument ... ]

parameters.name: program
parameters.description: The awk program text, unless -f supplies the program.

parameters.name: argument
parameters.description: An input file name, or - for standard input; an assignment can also be supplied.

parameters.name: sepstring
parameters.description: The input field separator.

parameters.name: progfile
parameters.description: A file containing awk program text.

parameters.name: assignment
parameters.description: A variable assignment processed before the program, including BEGIN actions.

awk.returns: The page does not define a normal return value. awk exits with a status; a valid program with no actions or patterns exits with status zero without reading input.

example.title: Print the first colon-separated field
example.explanation: This sets the input separator to a colon and prints the first field from each input record.

useCases.scenario: Select columns from structured text such as colon-separated system files.

useCases.title: Filter records
useCases.scenario: Run a rule for each input line that matches a condition.

useCases.title: Aggregate input
useCases.scenario: Set counters or configuration before reading input and print totals afterward.

useCases.title: Process files
useCases.scenario: Read several input files and apply the same pattern-action program.

interview.question: How does awk process input?
interview.answer: awk treats input as records and fields. A record is normally one line, and fields are split using FS or the -F option. Each matching pattern runs its action.
interview.followUp: How can record boundaries change? Set the RS built-in variable to a different separator.

interview.question: What are BEGIN and END used for?
interview.answer: BEGIN actions run before input records are processed. Normal pattern-action rules then process records in program order. END actions run after all input is exhausted.
interview.followUp: When should -v be used instead of a trailing assignment? Use -v when the value must be available before BEGIN actions.

interview.question: How do awk arrays work?
interview.answer: awk arrays are dynamic associative arrays. Their indexes are strings, and an index with comma-separated expressions is combined using SUBSEP. The in operator checks whether an element exists without creating it.
interview.followUp: What happens with another reference to a missing element? It creates that element automatically.

keyPoints: awk is a text-processing language driven by pattern and action pairs.
Input is normally processed one line at a time. RS can change the record separator.
Fields use a default whitespace separator. Set FS or use -F to choose another separator.
An action without a pattern runs for every input record.
BEGIN rules run before regular input processing, in the order written.
END rules run after the input files have been processed.
gotchas: A pattern without an action prints each matching record by default.
Assignments placed as command-line operands do not set variables before BEGIN; use -v when BEGIN must see the value.
Parenthesize a multi-part array index when testing it with in.

cat.summary: cat reads files in order and writes their contents to standard output. Without a file name, it reads standard input.
cat.explanation: cat reads each named file in order and writes its bytes to standard output. With no file name, or with -, it reads standard input. Options can add line numbers, show hidden characters, or reduce repeated empty lines.

parameters.name: OPTION
parameters.description: An option such as -n or --show-tabs.

parameters.name: FILE
parameters.description: A file to read. If omitted, cat reads standard input. A value of - means standard input at that position.

cat.returns: The command writes the input bytes to standard output. POSIX specifies exit status 0 when all input files are output successfully and a value greater than 0 when an error occurs.

example.title: Read files and standard input in sequence
example.explanation: This prints first.txt, then reads more text from standard input, then prints last.txt.

useCases.title: Concatenate files
useCases.scenario: Combine several text files into one output stream.

useCases.title: Read standard input
useCases.scenario: Pass typed or piped input through to another command.

useCases.title: Show invisible characters
useCases.scenario: Inspect line endings, tabs, or other nonprinting characters.

interview.question: What does cat do?
interview.answer: cat reads files in the order given and writes their contents to standard output. With no operands, it reads standard input.
interview.followUp: What does - mean? It selects standard input at that point in the input sequence.

interview.question: How do you number lines?
interview.answer: The -n option numbers every output line. The -b option numbers only nonempty lines and takes precedence over -n.
interview.followUp: How can repeated empty lines be reduced? Use -s to suppress repeated empty output lines.

interview.question: How can cat display otherwise hidden characters?
interview.answer: The GNU command supports options such as -A, -E, -T, and -v to show line endings, tabs, or nonprinting characters. The POSIX interface documents only -u, which requests output without delay.
interview.followUp: Why might -u matter? POSIX describes it as useful when prototyping non-blocking reads from FIFOs.

keyPoints: cat joins file contents and sends the result to standard output.
No file argument means that cat reads from standard input.
Use -b to number nonempty lines; it overrides -n.
Use -s to collapse runs of empty lines.
Use -T to display tab characters as ^I.
Use -v to show most nonprinting characters with caret and M- notation.
gotchas: Do not redirect cat output to the same file that is also an input. The shell can erase that file before cat reads it.
Using the same regular file for input and output can be treated as an error.

cd.summary: `cd` changes the current shell's working directory. It supports logical or physical handling of `..`, uses `HOME` or `OLDPWD` for special cases, and returns a nonzero status on error.
cd.explanation: `cd` changes the working directory of the current shell. With no argument, it uses `HOME`; `-` uses `OLDPWD`. Relative paths can use `CDPATH`, and `-L` keeps symbolic links logical while `-P` resolves them physically.

parameters.name: directory
parameters.description: An absolute or relative pathname of the directory that becomes the new working directory.

parameters.name: -L
parameters.description: Logical handling of `..`; this is the default when neither mode is given.

parameters.name: -P
parameters.description: Physical handling of `..` by resolving symbolic links first.

cd.returns: 0 when the directory changes successfully; greater than 0 when an error occurs.

example.title: Change directories and return
example.explanation: Enters `/tmp`, prints the location, returns to the previous directory, and prints that location.

useCases.title: Enter a directory
useCases.scenario: Move to a known absolute or relative directory in a shell script.

useCases.title: Switch to the previous directory
useCases.scenario: Return to the directory used before the last successful change.

useCases.title: Control path handling
useCases.scenario: Choose whether symbolic links affect the meaning of `..`.

interview.question: What does `cd` do, and how does it report failure?
interview.answer: `cd` changes the working directory of the current shell execution environment. It returns zero on success and a value greater than zero when an error occurs.
interview.followUp: Why does `cd` need to be a shell built-in? Because a separate process cannot change the parent shell's working directory.

interview.question: What do `cd` with no argument and `cd -` do?
interview.answer: Without an operand, `cd` uses the non-empty `HOME` value. `cd -` uses `OLDPWD`, then prints the new absolute path.
interview.followUp: What happens if `HOME` is unset or empty? The default behavior is implementation-defined, and no further steps are required.

interview.question: How do `-L` and `-P` differ?
interview.answer: `-L` handles `..` logically and does not resolve symbolic links first. `-P` resolves symbolic links before handling `..`; the default is logical handling.
interview.followUp: What if both options appear? The last of `-L` and `-P` takes effect.

keyPoints: The command changes the current shell's working directory.
With no directory argument, a non-empty `HOME` supplies the target directory.
`cd -` changes to the previous working directory named by `OLDPWD`.
`CDPATH` can provide directories used to find a relative target.
`-L` treats `..` logically, so symbolic links are not resolved before it is processed.
`-P` treats `..` physically by resolving symbolic links before processing it.
Exit status zero means the directory change succeeded.
Any exit status greater than zero means an error occurred.
gotchas: `cd` must run in the current shell to change the caller's directory. Running it in a subshell or separate utility does not change the caller's directory.
When both path modes are supplied, the last one wins.
A successful change can print a path when a non-empty `CDPATH` entry finds the directory.

cgroups.summary: Linux cgroups organize processes into hierarchical groups. Controllers can limit, monitor, account for, freeze, or resume resource use for those groups.
cgroups.explanation: The kernel exposes cgroups through a pseudo-filesystem. A cgroup is a directory in that filesystem, and controller files in the directory define limits, tracking, or other behavior. Processes can be moved by writing their process ID to cgroup.procs. Child cgroups inherit the hierarchy structure and are affected by settings above them.

example.title: Create and use a cgroup
example.explanation: This creates a cgroup, moves the current shell into it, and lists its member processes.

useCases.title: Resource limits
useCases.scenario: Apply CPU or memory controls to a group of processes.

useCases.title: Resource accounting
useCases.scenario: Measure CPU use for a set of processes.

useCases.title: Container isolation
useCases.scenario: Keep container processes from seeing ancestor cgroup paths.

interview.question: What are Linux cgroups?
interview.answer: Cgroups organize processes into hierarchical groups. Resource controllers then limit, monitor, account for, freeze, or resume those processes.
interview.followUp: How does the hierarchy affect settings? Settings at a higher level generally apply throughout the subhierarchy below that cgroup.

interview.question: How do cgroups v1 hierarchies work?
interview.answer: In cgroups v1, controllers can use separate hierarchies or share one hierarchy through a combined mount. A process can therefore have different cgroup paths for separately mounted controllers.
interview.followUp: Can one controller be mounted in two v1 hierarchies? No. The same controller cannot be used simultaneously in multiple v1 hierarchies.

interview.question: How do you create and populate a cgroup?
interview.answer: Create a directory in the cgroup filesystem, then write a process ID to the new directory's cgroup.procs file. Writing a PID moves that process into the cgroup and removes it from its previous cgroup in that hierarchy.
interview.followUp: What must happen before deletion? The cgroup must have no child cgroups and no nonzombie processes.

keyPoints: Cgroups group processes so the kernel can limit and monitor resource use.
Controllers implement resource-specific behavior, such as CPU or memory accounting and limits.
A controller's groups form a tree made from directories in the cgroup filesystem.
Create a cgroup by making a directory below the mounted cgroup filesystem.
Writing a PID to cgroup.procs moves the process from its old group to the selected group.
A cgroup namespace changes the cgroup paths visible through selected proc files.
gotchas: A controller cannot be used in more than one v1 hierarchy. Separate mount points may show the same hierarchy, but they do not create independent uses of the controller.
Before deleting a cgroup directory, remove its child cgroups and move its member processes elsewhere.
Write one process ID per cgroup.procs operation.

chmod.summary: chmod changes file permission bits. Use symbolic modes for selected changes or octal modes to set a complete permission pattern.
chmod.explanation: chmod changes permission bits on each named file. You can describe changes with symbolic modes, such as u+x, or set all permission bits with an octal mode, such as 755. It can also copy permissions from another file or apply changes recursively.
chmod.syntax:
chmod [ OPTION ]... MODE [ ,MODE ]... FILE ...
chmod [ OPTION ]... OCTAL-MODE FILE ...
chmod [ OPTION ]... --reference=RFILE FILE ...

parameters.name: OPTION
parameters.description: Options such as -R, --reference, and link-handling options documented by the command.

parameters.name: MODE
parameters.description: A symbolic mode, an octal mode, or a reference-file mode operation.

parameters.name: FILE
parameters.description: One or more files whose mode bits are changed.

parameters.name: RFILE
parameters.description: A file whose mode is used with --reference.

chmod.returns: The command returns a successful status when all requested changes are made; a status greater than zero means an error occurred.

example.title: Change file permissions
example.code:
chmod u=rw,go=r report.txt
chmod 755 script.sh
chmod -R o-w shared/
example.explanation: The first command gives the owner read and write access and gives the group and others read access. The second sets owner, group, and other permissions with an octal mode. The third removes write access for others throughout a directory tree.

useCases.title: Add execute permission
useCases.scenario: A script must be executable by its owner.

useCases.title: Set permissions with octal notation
useCases.scenario: A file needs a precise owner, group, and other permission pattern.

useCases.title: Change a hierarchy recursively
useCases.scenario: A directory tree needs one permission change applied to every contained file and directory.

useCases.title: Copy a mode from a reference file
useCases.scenario: Several files should receive the same mode as an existing file.

interview.question: What is the difference between symbolic and octal modes?
interview.answer: chmod changes file mode bits. A symbolic mode selects users, an operator, and permissions, for example u+x. An octal mode supplies the complete bit pattern, with special bits in the first digit and owner, group, and other permissions in the next three digits.
interview.followUp: What does X mean in a symbolic mode? X adds execute or search permission only when the path is a directory or some execute permission is already set.

interview.question: How do symbolic chmod modes work?
interview.answer: The users are u for the owner, g for the file's group, o for other users, and a for all users. The + operator adds bits, - removes them, and = sets selected bits while removing unmentioned bits, with a directory special-bit exception.
interview.followUp: What happens when no user class is written? The command acts like a, but permission bits masked by the process umask are not changed.

interview.question: How does recursive chmod handle symbolic links?
interview.answer: With -R, chmod changes a directory and the files in its hierarchy. Symbolic links encountered during recursive traversal are ignored, but a symbolic link named directly on the command line changes the permissions of its target.
interview.followUp: Can chmod always change a link's own permissions? No. The chmod system call cannot change symbolic-link permissions on most systems, and most systems ignore them.

keyPoints: chmod changes permission bits for every file named in the command.
You can combine several symbolic changes with commas, such as u+rw,go-rwx.
Use + to add permissions without removing other existing permissions.
In a four-digit octal mode, the second digit controls the owner's read, write, and execute bits.
The first octal digit controls special bits: set-user-ID, set-group-ID, and sticky.
The --reference option copies the mode from RFILE to the listed files.
gotchas: chmod does not change a symbolic link's own permissions. A symbolic link named directly on the command line affects its target, while links found during recursive traversal are ignored.
Numeric modes do not always clear special bits on directories unless you explicitly include the needed form.
The sticky-bit meaning is defined for directories; behavior for other file types is unspecified.

chown.summary: `chown` changes the user owner, group owner, or both for files. It also supports recursive changes and copying ownership from a reference file.
chown.explanation: `chown` changes the user owner, group owner, or both for one or more files. Give an owner, optionally followed by `:group`; omit either part to leave it unchanged, except a trailing colon after a symbolic owner selects that user’s login group. With `--reference`, it copies ownership from another file.

parameters.name: OWNER
parameters.type: user name or numeric user ID
parameters.description: The user name or numeric user ID to assign. It may be omitted when only the group should change.

parameters.name: GROUP
parameters.type: group name or numeric group ID
parameters.description: The group name or numeric group ID to assign. It may be omitted when the group should remain unchanged.

parameters.name: FILE
parameters.description: The file or files whose ownership should change.

parameters.name: RFILE
parameters.description: A file whose owner and group should be copied when using `--reference`.

chown.returns: The command exits successfully when all requested changes are made. A nonzero exit status indicates an error.

example.title: Change owner and group
example.explanation: The first command sets the owner and group of `/u`. The second recursively sets the owner of `/u` and its contents, changing symbolic links rather than their targets.

useCases.title: Assign an owner and group
useCases.scenario: Set both ownership fields on a file or directory.

useCases.title: Change a tree recursively
useCases.scenario: Apply ownership to a directory and its contents.

useCases.title: Copy ownership from a reference
useCases.scenario: Make several files match one known file’s ownership.

interview.question: What does `chown` change?
interview.answer: `chown` changes file ownership. A command such as `chown alice:developers file` sets both the user owner and group owner; `chown alice file` changes only the user owner.
interview.followUp: How can only the group be changed? Use `chown :developers file`; this has the same function as `chgrp`.

interview.question: How does recursive operation handle symbolic links?
interview.answer: `-R` applies the requested ownership change to a directory and every file below it. Recursive symbolic-link behavior is controlled by `-H`, `-L`, or `-P`; `-P` is the default for GNU `chown`.
interview.followUp: What is the difference between `-H` and `-L`? `-H` follows a directory symlink given directly on the command line, while `-L` follows every directory symlink encountered.

interview.question: How can ownership be copied from another file?
interview.answer: `--reference=RFILE` makes each target use the owner and group of `RFILE`. The alternative operand form is `OWNER[:GROUP]`, where names or numeric IDs can be used.
interview.followUp: What happens with `chown :group file`? Only the group changes, while the user owner remains unchanged.

keyPoints: The command can change the user owner, the group owner, or both for each named file.
Owner and group values may be names, such as `root`, or numeric user and group IDs.
`--reference=RFILE` copies both ownership values from the reference file to each target file.
`-c` reports only files whose ownership actually changed, while `-v` reports every processed file.
Use `-f` or its aliases to suppress most error messages.
`-h` changes a symbolic link itself instead of the file named by the link.
gotchas: By default, a symbolic-link argument changes the ownership of the file it points to, not the link itself. Use `-h` to target the link when the system supports changing link ownership.
For recursive operation, `-P` is the default traversal mode. It does not follow symbolic links encountered in the directory tree.
Leaving out the owner keeps the owner unchanged, and leaving out the group keeps the group unchanged. A colon after a symbolic owner is an exception because it selects that user’s login group.

cp.summary: cp copies files and directories. Options control recursion, metadata preservation, symbolic links, backups, and overwriting.
cp.explanation: cp copies one source to a destination, or several sources into a directory. With recursive mode, it copies directories and their contents. Options can preserve attributes, control symbolic-link handling, avoid overwriting, or create backups.
cp.syntax:
cp [ OPTION ]... [ -T ] SOURCE DEST
cp [ OPTION ]... SOURCE ... DIRECTORY
cp [ OPTION ]... -t DIRECTORY SOURCE ...

parameters.description: The file or directory to copy.

parameters.name: DEST
parameters.description: The output file or directory.

parameters.name: DIRECTORY
parameters.description: An existing directory that receives one or more sources.

parameters.name: OPTION
parameters.description: Options that change copying, link handling, preservation, and overwrite behavior.

cp.returns: The page does not specify a return value.

interview.question: What forms of command does cp support?
interview.answer: Use `cp SOURCE DEST` for one source, or `cp SOURCE... DIRECTORY` for several sources. Use `-r` or `--recursive` when the source is a directory.
interview.followUp: How can copying avoid overwriting existing files? Use `-n` for no-clobber behavior, or `-i` to ask before overwriting.

interview.question: What does archive mode do?
interview.answer: `-a` is archive mode. It is equivalent to recursive copying with link preservation and preservation of all attributes.
interview.followUp: How can only selected attributes be preserved? Use `--preserve=ATTR_LIST`, or use `--no-preserve=ATTR_LIST` to exclude attributes.

interview.question: How does cp handle symbolic links?
interview.answer: By default, cp follows symbolic links according to its link-handling rules. `-H` follows command-line links, `-L` always follows source links, and `-P` never follows them.
interview.followUp: Which option should be chosen when links must remain links? Use `-P`, also named `--no-dereference`.

keyPoints: It can copy multiple source paths into one existing destination directory.
Attributes-only mode changes destination metadata without copying file data.
The parents option recreates the source path below the destination directory.
Reflink mode controls whether the file system may use copy-on-write clones.
Backup mode saves an existing destination before replacing it.
gotchas: The keep-directory-symlink option can make copying follow an existing symbolic link to a directory.
Using copy-contents with recursive copying can read and copy special-file contents.

crontab.summary: A crontab schedules shell commands for specific times. Jobs run as the owner of the crontab, using five time fields followed by the command.
crontab.explanation: A crontab gives the cron daemon commands and the times to run them. Each job runs as the crontab owner. A job line has five time fields followed by the command: minute, hour, day of month, month, and day of week.
crontab.syntax: minute hour day-of-month month day-of-week command

parameters.name: minute
parameters.description: Minute field. Usually 0-59.

parameters.name: hour
parameters.description: Hour field. Usually 0-23.

parameters.name: day_of_month
parameters.description: Day of month field.

parameters.name: month
parameters.description: Month field. Numbers or three-letter month names.

parameters.name: day_of_week
parameters.description: Day of week field. Numbers or three-letter day names.

parameters.name: command
parameters.description: Command to execute after the five time fields.

crontab.returns: Cron runs the specified command at matching times. It can mail command output using the configured MAILTO behavior.

useCases.scenario: Run a backup or cleanup script on a fixed schedule.

useCases.title: Startup task
useCases.scenario: Run a command after the machine starts.

useCases.title: Time-zone scheduling
useCases.scenario: Schedule jobs for a particular time zone.

useCases.title: System-wide scheduling
useCases.scenario: Run system jobs for a named user from /etc/cron.d.

interview.question: What is the format of a cron command?
interview.answer: A cron command has five time fields followed by the command. The fields are minute, hour, day of month, month, and day of week. A command runs when the time fields match; when both day-of-month and day-of-week are restricted, either matching field can trigger it.
interview.followUp: How would you express every weekday at 22:00? Use 0 22 * * 1-5, followed by the command.

interview.question: How do lists, ranges, and steps work?
interview.answer: A list uses commas, such as 1,2,5,9. A range uses a hyphen, such as 8-11. A step uses a slash after a range or an asterisk, such as 0-23/2 or */2.
interview.followUp: Can names be used? Yes. The month and day-of-week fields accept the first three letters of names, without case sensitivity.

interview.question: How does /etc/cron.d differ from a user crontab?
interview.answer: Jobs in /etc/cron.d and /etc/crontab are system jobs, so they include a username after the five time fields and before the command. A personal crontab does not include that username field.
interview.followUp: What happens if the file is a symlink and it changes? With inotify, cron does not automatically notice changes in symlinked crontabs; send SIGHUP to reload them.

keyPoints: Users can create their own crontabs. Jobs run with the permissions of the crontab owner.
Cron supplies SHELL, LOGNAME, and HOME. You can override HOME and SHELL in the crontab.
Set CRON_TZ to make the schedule use a chosen time zone. Log timestamps still use the daemon's local time zone.
RANDOM_DELAY adds a random startup delay up to its configured limit. The scaling factor stays fixed while the daemon runs.
Special forms include @reboot, @hourly, @daily, @weekly, @monthly, @yearly, and @annually.
The command runs through /bin/sh by default, or through the shell named by SHELL.
gotchas: Do not put an inline comment after a command. Cron treats it as part of the command.
An unescaped percent sign is special. It becomes a newline, and the text after the first one is sent to standard input.
End the file with a newline. Without it, cron may treat the file as partly broken.
A step such as */35 in the minute field runs at minute 0 and 35 of each hour. It does not mean every 35 minutes.

curl.summary: curl is a command-line tool for transferring data to or from servers through URLs. It supports many protocols and can print received data or save it to files.
curl.explanation: curl transfers data to or from a server by using a URL. It accepts options and one or more URLs, processes URLs in order by default, and writes received data to standard output unless an output option selects a file.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: Command-line options that control the transfer.

parameters.name: URLs
parameters.description: One or more URLs to transfer.

curl.returns: The received data is written to standard output by default, or to a local file when an output option is used. curl also returns an exit status that reports command success or failure.

example.title: Save a response

interview.question: What is curl used for?
interview.answer: curl is a command-line tool for transferring data to or from a server using URLs. It uses libcurl for transfer features and supports many URL schemes, including HTTP, HTTPS, FTP, and SFTP.
interview.followUp: How does curl handle several URLs? It fetches them in the given order by default, attempts connection reuse, and can use --parallel for parallel transfers.

interview.question: Where does curl write downloaded data?
interview.answer: Without an output option, curl writes received data to standard output. Use -o or --output for a chosen local filename, or -O or --remote-name to use a name derived from the remote URL.
interview.followUp: Does curl decode response content automatically? No. It does not encode or decode transferred content unless a dedicated option requests it.

interview.question: What is curl's command syntax?
interview.answer: The basic command form is curl [options / URLs]. Options can appear before, after, or between URLs, and a non-option argument is treated as a URL.
interview.followUp: What does --next change? It resets most option state so the next transfer starts with a clean set of non-global options.

keyPoints: curl transfers data between a client and a server through URLs.
A command can contain multiple URLs.
Multiple URLs run in the order given unless --parallel is used.
For transfers in one invocation, curl tries to reuse connections to reduce connection setup work.
The default destination for received data is standard output.
Use --output or --remote-name to save received data locally.
Use --globoff when bracket or brace characters should remain literal instead of creating URL patterns.
gotchas: A URL without a scheme can make curl choose a protocol based on the URL. Use an explicit scheme when the protocol matters.
Shells may interpret special URL characters such as braces, brackets, ampersands, question marks, and asterisks. Quote the full URL or use --globoff.
When downloading several URLs, provide separate output destinations as needed; one output option does not automatically define distinct filenames for every transfer.

interview.question: What does `cut` do, and what selection options can it use?
interview.answer: `cut` selects bytes, characters, or fields from each input line. Use exactly one of `-b`, `-c`, `-f`, or `-F`.
interview.followUp: How do you select fields separated by a comma? Use `cut -d, -fN`, replacing `N` with the one-based field number or range.

interview.question: How does field selection work?
interview.answer: `-d` changes the field separator from TAB to the given delimiter. `-f` then selects one or more fields.
interview.followUp: How can lines without the delimiter be excluded? Add `-s`, which tells `cut` not to print non-delimited lines.

interview.question: How are selection lists and ranges written?
interview.answer: A list contains one or more comma-separated ranges. A number selects one position, `N-` runs from position `N` to the end, `N-M` includes both endpoints, and `-M` runs through `M`.
interview.followUp: Are positions zero-based? No. The manual defines positions as counted from 1.

keyPoints: `cut` prints selected parts of every input line.
It reads standard input when no file is supplied or when the file argument is `-`.
Use `-b LIST` to select byte positions.
Use `-c LIST` to select character positions.
Use `-f LIST` to select delimiter-separated fields.
A selection list can contain one range or several comma-separated ranges.
gotchas: Choose exactly one selection mode: bytes, characters, fields, or the special field mode.
Field mode normally prints lines without the delimiter. Add `-s` to omit those lines.
Overlapping or repeated ranges do not duplicate selected input.

Daemons.explanation: A daemon is a background service that supervises the system or provides functions to other processes. For modern Linux systems, a daemon should use the service manager instead of manually detaching, and should report status, handle signals, use activation when suitable, and return useful exit codes.
Daemons.returns: The main daemon process should return an exit code that indicates success or failure to the service manager.

interview.question: What is a daemon, and how should modern daemons start?
interview.answer: A daemon is a background service that supervises the system or provides functions to other processes. Modern daemons should use the service manager rather than manually forking and detaching.
interview.followUp: Why should a new-style daemon avoid traditional daemonization? The service manager already provides a clean process context and needs to monitor the original process and manage its file descriptors.

interview.question: How should a new-style daemon communicate its state?
interview.answer: A daemon should notify the service manager when startup finishes, handle SIGTERM by shutting down cleanly, reload configuration on SIGHUP when applicable, and return a useful exit code. It should also expose status when possible.
interview.followUp: What notification sequence can describe a reload? Send RELOADING=1, reload the configuration, then send READY=1.

interview.question: What is socket-based activation?
interview.answer: Socket activation moves creation and binding of listening sockets from the daemon into the service manager. The manager passes the sockets to the daemon, which can start on demand and keep requests queued during restart.
interview.followUp: What must a socket-activated daemon change? It must accept sockets from the service manager instead of creating and binding them itself.

keyPoints: A daemon runs in the background and provides a service to the system or to other processes.
Modern daemons should follow the new-style service model provided by systemd.
Handle SIGTERM by stopping cleanly.
Handle SIGHUP by reloading configuration when the daemon supports reloading.
Return an accurate exit code so the service manager can detect errors.
A new-style daemon can write logs to standard error for forwarding by the service manager.
gotchas: Do not use the BSD daemon() function when full SysV compatibility is needed.
Do not repeat SysV startup steps under a new-style service; they can interfere with monitoring and file-descriptor passing.
Use O_NOCTTY when opening possible terminal devices so the daemon does not acquire a controlling terminal.

interview.question: What does df report?
interview.answer: df reports space for the file system containing each path. Without a path, it reports all currently mounted file systems.
interview.followUp: What happens for a device node? If the absolute path names a device node containing a mounted file system, df reports that device's file system.

interview.question: What units does df use?
interview.answer: By default, GNU df uses 1024-byte units. POSIXLY_CORRECT changes the default to 512-byte blocks, and block-size environment variables can also select the display unit.
interview.followUp: How do you request readable values? Use -h for powers of 1024 or -H for powers of 1000.

interview.question: How can df show inode usage and file system type?
interview.answer: Use -i to show inode totals, used inodes, available inodes, and inode percentage instead of block usage. Use -T to add the file system type.
interview.followUp: How can output be made stable for scripts? POSIX df supports -P for a portable format; GNU df also supports --output with selected fields.

keyPoints: A path makes df report the file system that contains that path.
GNU df normally displays space in 1K blocks.
Use -h when sizes should use readable binary units such as M and G.
Use -H when sizes should use decimal powers of 1000.
Use -i to inspect inode capacity rather than storage-block capacity.
Use -l to exclude non-local file systems from the listing.
Use -t to include only a selected file system type.
Use -x to omit a selected file system type.
gotchas: df cannot report free space for an unmounted file system.
Running df without a path includes all currently mounted file systems.
Use --sync only when you want df to run sync before collecting usage data; --no-sync is the default.

interview.answer: Run csysdig without arguments for live data. Use -r with a trace file to inspect saved events.
interview.followUp: How can the update interval be changed? Use -d with milliseconds; the default is 2000.

interview.question: How does csysdig show container information?

interview.followUp: How would you connect csysdig to Kubernetes? Use -k with the API server address, or set SYSDIG_K8S_API.

Using --exclude-users prevents those tables from being created, so related user and group fields cannot be used.
Container columns appear only when the container-friendly option is enabled.

interview.question: What does du do?
interview.answer: du estimates space used by the specified files and recursively processes directories. Its default output reports totals for directories rather than every file.
interview.followUp: How do you report every file? Use --all, which adds non-directory files to the output.

interview.question: What is the difference between device usage and apparent size?
interview.answer: Use --apparent-size to report file sizes instead of allocated device usage. Use --bytes as shorthand for apparent size with a block size of one byte.
interview.followUp: Why can apparent size be larger? Sparse-file holes and filesystem metadata such as indirect blocks can affect the values.

interview.question: How does du handle symbolic links?
interview.answer: Use --dereference to follow all symbolic links, or --dereference-args to follow only links given on the command line. Without these options, symbolic links are not followed.
interview.followUp: How can traversal stay on one filesystem? Add --one-file-system to skip directories on other filesystems.

Use -h or --human-readable for compact units such as K, M, and G.
--max-depth=N limits output to entries no deeper than N levels below each argument.
Use -c or --total to add one combined total after processing all operands.
--inodes reports inode counts rather than block usage.
--exclude=PATTERN omits matching files and directories during traversal.
gotchas: Allocated device usage and apparent file size are different. Sparse files can make apparent size larger.
The --exclude pattern uses shell-style matching, not regular expressions.
Use --one-file-system when traversal must stay on the starting filesystem.

env.explanation: env changes the environment for a command, then runs that command. You can add or remove variables, start with no inherited variables, change the working directory, and control selected signal handling. Without a command, it prints the resulting environment.

interview.question: What does env do?
interview.answer: env builds an environment from the current one, applies NAME=VALUE changes and options, and then runs the command. With no command, it prints the resulting environment.
interview.followUp: How can you remove an inherited variable? Use -u NAME before the command.

interview.question: What is the difference between env and env -i?
interview.answer: The -i option starts with an empty environment. Variables given as NAME=VALUE are then added before the command runs.
interview.followUp: What is a common risk? A command may need variables such as PATH or locale settings that are no longer inherited.

interview.question: How are exit statuses reported?
interview.answer: If the command cannot be found, env returns 127. If it is found but cannot be invoked, env returns 126; otherwise it returns the command's status.
interview.followUp: What status reports a failure inside env itself? The GNU manual specifies 125.

Without a command, env prints the environment it would use.
Use -i to ignore all inherited environment variables.
Use -u NAME to remove one variable before starting the command.

Use -S to split one string into several arguments, including in a shebang.

Exit status 126 means the command was found but could not be started.
Exit status 127 means the command could not be found.

Exit codes.explanation: The POSIX `command` utility makes the shell execute a simple command while skipping shell function lookup. Its `-v` and `-V` forms report how the shell would resolve a command. It is commonly used inside shell functions and scripts when the command must be found without selecting a function with the same name.

  echo "tool is available"
else

fi

interview.question: What does the `command` utility do?
interview.answer: `command` runs a simple command while suppressing shell function lookup. This lets a script call the command found by normal command search instead of a function with the same name.
interview.followUp: How can a script check for a command without running it? Use `command -v name`; the result depends on the current shell execution environment.

interview.question: What are `command -v` and `command -V` used for?
interview.answer: The `-v` and `-V` options report how the shell resolves a command name. They can identify a pathname or describe a built-in, depending on the command.
interview.followUp: Why might the result differ under `nohup`? A separate utility environment may not know the current shell's aliases, functions, or special built-ins.

interview.question: What do exit statuses 126 and 127 mean?
interview.answer: Status 127 indicates that the command could not be found or execution attempts failed because it was absent. Status 126 indicates that the command was found but could not be invoked.
interview.followUp: Why does this distinction matter? Scripts can show different error messages for a missing command and an unusable command.

keyPoints: `command` tells the shell to process its arguments as one simple command.
It prevents a shell function from being selected during command lookup.
The basic form accepts an optional `-p`, a command name, and zero or more arguments.
The `-v` and `-V` forms inspect how the shell resolves a command name.
Shells generally provide this utility as a regular built-in so it can inspect the current execution environment.
gotchas: `command -v` may give incomplete or incorrect information when used in a separate execution environment, such as through `nohup`.
A command that cannot be found normally uses status 127; a command that is found but cannot be invoked normally uses 126.

export.explanation: The shell marks named variables for export. Later commands started by the shell receive those variables in their environment. A name followed by =word is assigned that value before it is exported. The -p option prints exported variables in shell-readable form.

interview.question: What does export do?
interview.answer: export gives variables the export attribute. Commands started later by the shell then receive those variables in their environment. It can also assign a value when written as name=word.
interview.followUp: How can exported variables reach a child process? A new process receives the environment when it is started, and a child made with fork inherits a copy of its parent's environment.

interview.question: What is the purpose of -p?
interview.answer: export -p writes exported variables and their values to standard output. The shell quotes the output so it can be read again as commands with the same exporting results, with documented limits for read-only and previously unset variables.
interview.followUp: What is the portable way to save and restore exports? Redirect export -p to a file, then source that file after changing the shell state.

interview.question: What exit statuses can export return?
interview.answer: The command exits with status 0 when all names were exported successfully. It exits with a status greater than 0 if a name could not be exported, or if -p encountered an error.
interview.followUp: What happens with export X=$(false)? The export command can return 0 because it successfully assigns an empty value; use X=$(false) followed by export X to detect the substitution failure.

keyPoints: Exported variables are passed to commands that the shell starts afterward.
Use name=word to set a variable's value while also exporting it.
With -p, a set exported variable is shown with its name and value.
With -p, an exported variable without a value is shown by name only.
The -p output is formatted so it can be entered back into the shell.
Diagnostic messages from export are written to standard error.
A zero exit status means every supplied name was exported successfully.
gotchas: Do not use export alone to detect a command substitution failure. Separate the assignment from the export so the assignment's status can be checked.
The behavior of export with no arguments is not portable. Use export -p when you need to list exported variables.

find.explanation: find walks each starting directory and evaluates an expression for every name. Tests and actions are read from left to right, with implicit AND when no operator is written; traversal continues when the result is known.

interview.question: How does find process an expression?
interview.answer: find searches the directory tree below each starting point. It evaluates the expression for each file from left to right and stops evaluating when the result is already known.
interview.followUp: What happens when no starting point is given? The current directory, ., is used.

interview.question: How does find handle symbolic links?
interview.answer: -P is the default and does not follow symbolic links. -L follows them, including links to directories; -H follows symbolic links given as command-line starting points.
interview.followUp: Which link option wins if several are present? The last of -H, -L, and -P takes effect.

interview.question: What are the main parts of a find expression?
interview.answer: Tests check file properties, operators combine expression parts, and actions can have side effects. An action such as -print normally prevents find from adding its default output.
interview.followUp: Why use -print0? It emits NUL-separated names, which are safer for names containing unusual characters when another program consumes the output.

find evaluates tests and actions from left to right, subject to operator precedence.

Use -print0 when another program reads the output. It separates names with NUL characters.
If you omit the starting path, find searches the current directory.
When you provide several link options, the last one on the command line wins.

useCases.scenario: Compare physical memory and swap usage.

interview.question: What does free do?
interview.answer: free displays free and used physical and swap memory. It also shows buffers and caches used by the kernel.
interview.followUp: Which source provides the data? It parses /proc/meminfo.

interview.question: How do used, free, and available differ?
interview.answer: used is calculated as total minus available. free is unused memory from MemFree or SwapFree, while available estimates memory that applications can use without swapping.
interview.followUp: Why can available be larger than free? Reclaimable page cache and some reclaimable slabs can be used without swapping.

interview.question: How can output units be changed?
interview.answer: The default unit is kibibytes. Use -m for mebibytes, -g for gibibytes, -b for bytes, or --si to use decimal powers of 1000.
interview.followUp: What does -s do? It repeatedly displays the result after a delay, using microsecond-resolution timing internally.

keyPoints: The command reports physical memory and swap totals, including free and used amounts.
free gets its statistics by reading and parsing /proc/meminfo.
The used column means total memory minus available memory.
available estimates how much memory new applications can use without causing swapping.
buff/cache combines kernel buffers with page-cache and reclaimable-slab memory.
Use -t or --total to print an additional totals line.
gotchas: With memory overcommit enabled, the commit view can show a negative free value. This indicates promised virtual memory above the total address space, not a command failure.
On kernels older than 2.6.32, shared is shown as zero because that statistic is unavailable.

grep.summary: grep prints input lines that match one or more patterns. It can search files, standard input, or directory trees.
grep.explanation: grep reads input files line by line and prints lines that match one or more patterns. Without a file argument, it reads standard input; a file name of - also means standard input.
grep.syntax:
grep [OPTION]... PATTERNS [FILE]...
grep [OPTION]... -e PATTERNS ... [FILE]...
grep [OPTION]... -f PATTERN_FILE ... [FILE]...

parameters.name: PATTERNS
parameters.description: One or more search patterns. In the first form, patterns are separated by newline characters.

parameters.name: FILE
parameters.description: Files to search. A value of - means standard input.

grep.returns: Exit status 0 if a line is selected, 1 if no lines are selected, and 2 if an error occurred.

example.title: Find marked work
example.explanation: Prints each line in app.txt that contains TODO, with its line number.

useCases.title: Search source files
useCases.scenario: Find lines containing a text pattern in one or more files.

useCases.title: Test command output
useCases.scenario: Check whether a command output contains a required value using grep's exit status.

useCases.title: Search a directory tree
useCases.scenario: Search all files below a directory and limit results with matching options.

interview.question: What does grep do?
interview.answer: grep searches input files for matching patterns and normally prints each matching line. If no file is supplied, it reads standard input.
interview.followUp: How can you search subdirectories? Use -r for recursive searching, or -R when all symbolic links should be followed.

interview.question: How do grep pattern modes differ?
interview.answer: The default syntax is basic regular expressions. Use -E for extended regular expressions, -F for fixed strings, or -P for Perl-compatible expressions when supported.
interview.followUp: What is a safe choice for literal user input? Use -F, and use -e when the pattern could start with a dash.

interview.question: What are grep's exit statuses?
interview.answer: grep exits with 0 when it selects at least one line, 1 when it selects no lines, and 2 when an error occurs. The -q option exits as soon as it finds a match and writes nothing.
interview.followUp: What does -c do with -v? It counts lines that do not match instead of lines that match.

keyPoints: It searches each named file for the given patterns.
Use - as a file name to read from standard input explicitly.
Use -F when the pattern should be treated as literal text.
Use -r to search directory contents recursively without following every symbolic link.
Use -n to show the line number before each matching line.
Use -l to print matching file names instead of matching lines.
gotchas: Quote patterns in shell commands so the shell does not interpret special pattern characters first.
An exit status of 1 means that no line matched. An exit status of 2 means an error occurred.
Character ranges such as [a-d] can behave differently by locale. Use the C locale when you need the traditional range meaning.

gzip.summary: rpm2archive converts RPM packages into tar archives. It can read a package file or an RPM stream from standard input.
gzip.explanation: rpm2archive reads RPM packages and writes tar archives to standard output. You can give an RPM file as an argument or use - to read an RPM stream from standard input. The default archive format is pax, and output is gzip-compressed when standard output is a terminal.

parameters.name: FILES
parameters.description: RPM package file, or - to read an RPM stream from standard input.

parameters.name: -n, --nocompression
parameters.description: Create an uncompressed tar archive.

parameters.name: -f, --format=pax|cpio
parameters.description: Choose pax or cpio output.

gzip.returns: A tar archive written to standard output; it is gzip-compressed by default in the documented terminal-output case.

example.explanation: Converts an RPM package to a gzip-compressed tar stream and extracts it with tar.

useCases.title: Process streamed input
useCases.scenario: An RPM package is arriving through a pipe.

useCases.title: Handle large package files
useCases.scenario: A package may contain files larger than 4 GB.

interview.question: What does rpm2archive do?
interview.answer: rpm2archive converts one or more RPM inputs into tar archives on standard output. It can also read an RPM stream from standard input when the input argument is -.
interview.followUp: How can it process a package from a pipeline? Pipe the RPM bytes to rpm2archive - and then pipe its tar output to tar.

interview.question: Which archive formats does it support?
interview.answer: The default output format is pax. The -f option can select either pax or cpio.
interview.followUp: Why is pax usually safer for large packages? Unlike cpio here, pax can represent files larger than 4 GB.

interview.question: How do you disable compression?
interview.answer: By default, rpm2archive creates gzip-compressed tar output in the terminal-output case. Use --nocompression to create an uncompressed tar archive and use the .tar postfix.
interview.followUp: What command extracts the default stream? Pipe it to tar -xvz, where -z tells tar to handle gzip compression.

keyPoints: Give RPM file names as arguments. The command writes tar archive data to standard output.
Use - as the input name to read an RPM stream from standard input.
The -n or --nocompression option disables gzip compression.
The -f option chooses pax or cpio output.
pax is the default archive format; cpio is available for compatibility.
The tool supports RPM packages containing files larger than 4 GB.
gotchas: Do not use the cpio output format when the package can contain files larger than 4 GB.
When output goes directly to a terminal, the command writes a .tgz file instead of a raw archive stream.

head.summary: head prints the beginning of files. It shows the first 10 lines by default and can instead select a chosen number of lines or bytes.
head.explanation: head reads each named file and writes its beginning to standard output. By default, it writes ten lines. Without a file name, or when the file name is -, it reads standard input. With several files, it normally prints a file-name header before each file.

parameters.name: OPTION
parameters.description: Options such as -n, -c, -q, -v, and -z control the selected data and headers.

parameters.name: FILE
parameters.description: An input file. Use - or omit FILE to read standard input.

parameters.name: NUM
parameters.description: A count, optionally with a size suffix. A leading minus selects all but the final count.

head.returns: On successful completion, head exits with status 0. A status greater than 0 indicates an error.

example.title: Show the first five lines
example.explanation: Prints the first five lines of app.log.

useCases.title: Preview a file
useCases.scenario: Quickly inspect a log or configuration file without opening the whole file.

useCases.title: Limit pipeline output
useCases.scenario: Send a command's output into head to keep only its beginning.

useCases.title: Process NUL-delimited input
useCases.scenario: Read records separated by NUL bytes.

interview.question: What does head do by default?
interview.answer: head writes the beginning of each input file. It uses ten lines by default, and -n changes the line count.
interview.followUp: How can you select data by bytes instead? Use -c NUM; a leading minus excludes the final NUM bytes.

interview.question: How does head read standard input?
interview.answer: The command reads standard input when no file is supplied or when the file operand is -. This supports pipelines and interactive input.
interview.followUp: What happens with multiple files? head normally prints a header containing each file name before its output.

interview.question: How do you choose lines or bytes?
interview.answer: Use -n NUM for lines and -c NUM for bytes. NUM can include decimal or binary size suffixes, such as kB or KiB.
interview.followUp: How can headers be controlled? -q suppresses them, while -v always prints them.

keyPoints: The default output is the first ten lines of every input file.
Use -c NUM to limit output by bytes rather than by lines.
Use -n NUM to choose how many lines head prints.
The quiet option removes file-name headers.
The verbose option forces file-name headers, including when one file is read.
A missing file operand or - makes head consume standard input.
gotchas: A negative line count means everything except the last NUM lines. It does not mean that NUM is invalid.
Several input files produce name headers unless you disable them with -q.
Use -z when records are separated by NUL bytes instead of newline characters.

HOME.summary: HOME is an environment variable for a user's login directory. It is passed to a process when the process starts and copied to a child created with fork.
HOME.explanation: HOME stores the logged-in user's login directory. A process receives environment variables when it starts, and a child made with fork inherits a copy of its parent's environment. Programs can read HOME like other name-value environment entries.

example.title: Read HOME in a shell
example.explanation: Prints the value of the HOME environment variable.

useCases.title: Locate the login directory
useCases.scenario: A program needs to find a user's default files or configuration directory.

useCases.title: Pass user context to a process
useCases.scenario: A shell starts a program that needs the user's home path.

interview.question: What does HOME represent?
interview.answer: HOME is an environment variable that identifies a user's login directory. It is normally set when the user changes through a session-management interface.
interview.followUp: What happens to environment variables after fork? A child receives a copy of the parent process's environment.

interview.question: How does a shell pass HOME to a program?
interview.answer: A shell can place variables in its environment with export. A program started by that shell can then receive those variables when it starts.
interview.followUp: How can a program change its environment? It can use functions such as setenv, putenv, or unsetenv, which are listed in the manual's related interfaces.

interview.question: What is the format of an environment entry?
interview.answer: Environment entries conventionally use the form name=value. The name is case-sensitive and cannot contain an equals sign; neither part can contain an embedded null byte.
interview.followUp: Why can an environment entry not contain a null byte? The null byte terminates the string representation used for the entry.

keyPoints: Environment entries normally use name=value form.
Variable names are case-sensitive and cannot contain an equals sign.
The environ array ends with a NULL pointer.
A forked child receives a copy of the parent's environment.
In sh, export adds a variable to the shell environment for started programs.
HOME identifies the user's login directory.
gotchas: Do not assume HOME always describes the original user. Session-management programs can change it, and switching users may leave a mixed environment.

htop.summary: htop is an interactive terminal process viewer. It shows processes and lets you inspect, select, and manage them without typing their process IDs.
htop.explanation: htop displays running processes in a terminal interface. You can scroll through processes, view command arguments or a tree, select several processes, and perform actions such as killing or changing priority without entering process IDs.

parameters.name: DELAY
parameters.description: Refresh delay in tenths of a second.

parameters.name: FILTER
parameters.description: Fixed command terms used to filter processes. Separate multiple terms with |.

parameters.name: PID,PID...
parameters.description: One or more process IDs to display.

htop.returns: Displays the interactive process viewer and exits after a help request or normal quit.

example.title: Limit the process view
example.explanation: Starts htop with a 2-second update delay and shows only processes 1234 and 5678.

useCases.title: Inspect processes
useCases.scenario: Find and inspect a running program and its command arguments.

useCases.title: Manage process groups
useCases.scenario: Select several related processes and apply one action to them.

useCases.title: Narrow the process list
useCases.scenario: Watch only selected process IDs or commands.

interview.question: What is htop, and how does it differ from top?
interview.answer: htop is an interactive, ncurses-based process viewer. Unlike top, it supports vertical and horizontal scrolling, mouse input, tree views, multi-process selection, and process actions without typing PIDs.
interview.followUp: How can you limit the displayed processes? Use the --pid option for specific PIDs or --filter for case-insensitive fixed-string command matching.

interview.question: How do you control htop's refresh interval?
interview.answer: Use -d or --delay with a value in tenths of a second. Values below 1 become 1, and values above 100 become 100.
interview.followUp: What is the fastest supported refresh interval? One tenth of a second, because the delay is clamped to 1 in the tenths-of-a-second unit.

interview.question: How can htop operate on several processes?
interview.answer: Press Space to tag or untag the selected process. Press c to tag the process and its children. Multi-process commands, such as kill, then use the tagged set instead of only the highlighted process.
interview.followUp: How can all tags be removed? Press U, which removes tags made with Space or c.

keyPoints: htop is a terminal process viewer that uses ncurses.
The process list can show every process running on the system.
A tree view shows process parent and child relationships.
Use --filter to match fixed command terms without regular expressions; matching ignores case.
Use --pid to restrict the display to selected process IDs.
Space toggles a tag on the selected process.
gotchas: The update delay uses tenths of a second and cannot be set below 0.1 seconds.
Do not edit the configuration file by hand. Setup changes can overwrite it when htop exits normally.
Exit cleanly if you want configuration changes to be saved.

Inodes.summary: An inode stores metadata about a file. Applications can read it with stat() or statx().
Inodes.explanation: An inode stores metadata for a file. Programs read this metadata with stat() or statx(). It includes the file's device, inode number, type, permissions, owner, timestamps, link count, and size. The inode describes the file, while directory entries connect names to inode numbers.
Inodes.returns: stat() returns a stat structure; statx() returns a statx structure containing inode metadata.

example.title: View inode metadata
example.explanation: This command displays metadata for file.txt, including inode information.

useCases.title: File inspection
useCases.scenario: Inspect a file's metadata from a shell.

useCases.title: Identity checks
useCases.scenario: Compare file identity within one filesystem.

useCases.title: Programmatic metadata access
useCases.scenario: Read ownership, permissions, timestamps, and size in a program.

useCases.scenario: Use a memory-backed filesystem for temporary data.

interview.question: What is an inode?
interview.answer: An inode is filesystem metadata associated with a file. It records properties such as the inode number, file type, permissions, owner, timestamps, link count, and size.
interview.followUp: What connects a filename to an inode? A directory entry maps the name to the inode number; multiple names can refer to the same inode through hard links.

interview.question: How can a program read inode information?
interview.answer: Use stat() or a related call to retrieve a stat structure, or use statx() to retrieve a statx structure. These calls expose inode metadata to applications.
interview.followUp: Why might an application use statx()? It can request the statx fields and information supported by the filesystem and kernel, rather than relying only on the older stat structure.

interview.question: What do the device and inode fields identify?
interview.answer: The device identifies where the inode resides. Its major ID identifies the device class, and its minor ID identifies a particular device in that class.
interview.followUp: Is the inode number enough to identify a file everywhere? No. It is unique within one filesystem, so the filesystem or device must also be considered.

keyPoints: Every file has an inode that stores information about the file.
Applications can read inode metadata with stat(), related calls, or statx().
The inode is stored in a filesystem on a device identified by major and minor IDs.
stat.st_ino and statx.stx_ino report the inode number.
Files have unique inode numbers inside their filesystem.
tmpfs keeps filesystem contents in virtual memory instead of ordinary persistent storage.
gotchas: An inode number is unique only within its filesystem. Do not treat it as a system-wide file identifier.
Files in tmpfs, including their inodes, disappear when the filesystem is unmounted.

ip.summary: `ip address` manages IPv4 and IPv6 addresses attached to network devices. It can display, add, change, replace, delete, save, and flush addresses.
ip.explanation: The ip command works with network objects such as addresses, links, routes, and neighbors. For addresses, it can display, add, change, replace, delete, save, or flush protocol addresses attached to a device. The command supports filters such as device, scope, prefix, address type, and state.
ip.syntax:
ip [ OPTIONS ] address { COMMAND | help }
ip address { add | change | replace } IFADDR dev IFNAME [ LIFETIME ] [ CONFFLAG-LIST ]
ip address del IFADDR dev IFNAME [ mngtmpaddr ]
ip address { save | flush } [ dev IFNAME ] [ scope SCOPE-ID ] [ metric METRIC ] [ to PREFIX ] [ FLAG-LIST ] [ label PATTERN ] [ up ]
ip address [ show [ dev IFNAME ] [ scope SCOPE-ID ] [ to PREFIX ] [ FLAG-LIST ] [ label PATTERN ] [ master DEVICE ] [ type TYPE ] [ vrf NAME ] [ up ] [ nomaster ] [ proto ADDRPROTO ] ]

parameters.name: IFADDR
parameters.description: An IPv4 or IPv6 address, optionally followed by a prefix length.

parameters.name: IFNAME
parameters.description: The network device that owns the address.

parameters.name: LFT
parameters.description: The address lifetime, in seconds or `forever`.

parameters.name: SCOPE-ID
parameters.description: The address scope, such as `host`, `link`, `global`, or a number.

ip.returns: The command returns output for display operations. The `ip` utility exits with status 0 on success, 1 for a syntax error, and 2 when the kernel reports an error.

example.title: Manage an IPv6 address
example.code:
ip address add 2001:db8:85a3::370:7334/64 dev eth1
ip address show dev eth1
ip address delete 2001:db8:85a3::370:7334/64 dev eth1
example.explanation: Adds an IPv6 address to eth1, displays addresses on that device, then removes the address.

useCases.scenario: Assign an address to a network interface.

useCases.scenario: Find addresses by scope, prefix, type, or state.

interview.question: What does ip address manage?
interview.answer: The address object manages IPv4 and IPv6 addresses attached to network devices. Common actions include show, add, change, replace, delete, save, and flush.
interview.followUp: How can you limit displayed addresses? Use selectors such as dev, scope, to, label, type, vrf, up, or nomaster.

interview.question: How do you add an address?
interview.answer: Use `ip address add ADDRESS dev IFNAME`. The address can include a prefix length, such as `/64` for IPv6.
interview.followUp: What happens if you add `noprefixroute`? The kernel does not automatically create a route for the address's network prefix.

interview.question: How do you inspect assigned addresses?
interview.answer: `ip address show` lists protocol addresses. Selectors can restrict the output to one device, scope, prefix, label, interface type, or running interface.
interview.followUp: How can you find addresses that failed IPv6 duplicate address detection? Add the `dadfailed` selector.

keyPoints: An address belongs to a network device and uses either IPv4 or IPv6 format.
The address object can inspect, create, and remove protocol addresses.
IPv4 addresses use dotted decimal notation. IPv6 addresses use hexadecimal groups separated by colons.
`valid_lft` controls how long the kernel keeps an address. `preferred_lft` controls whether new outgoing connections use it.
An address scope says where an address is valid, such as `global`, `link`, or `host`.
gotchas: Use address flush carefully. It removes every address selected by the filters.
Deleting an address without its address arguments can remove the device's first address.
Removing an address can stop a device from using that protocol.

journalctl.summary: journalctl prints entries stored in the systemd journal. Use options and FIELD=VALUE matches to inspect logs for a unit, boot, process, or other journal data.
journalctl.explanation: journalctl reads entries stored by systemd-journald.service and systemd-journal-remote.service. With no arguments, it shows accessible entries from oldest to newest. Options and FIELD=VALUE matches can restrict which entries are shown.

parameters.name: OPTIONS... [MATCHES...]
parameters.description: Options and FIELD=VALUE match expressions used to select and format journal entries.

journalctl.returns: Prints selected journal entries. In follow mode, it continues until interrupted.

example.explanation: Shows recent entries for apache.service and keeps printing new entries until stopped with Ctrl-C.

useCases.scenario: Inspect all accessible system logs in time order.

useCases.title: Follow a service
useCases.scenario: Watch new messages from a running service.

useCases.title: Compare boots
useCases.scenario: Investigate messages from an earlier system boot.

useCases.title: Search structured logs
useCases.scenario: Filter entries by unit, process, or structured field.

interview.question: What does journalctl do?
interview.answer: journalctl prints log entries stored in the systemd journal. Without arguments, it shows entries available to the caller, beginning with the oldest entry.
interview.followUp: How can output be restricted to one service? Use -u or --unit with the unit name, such as journalctl -u apache.service.

interview.question: How are match arguments combined?
interview.answer: Different field matches are combined with logical AND. Repeated matches for the same field are alternatives, and a separate + word combines groups with logical OR.
interview.followUp: How would you match two fields for one process or either of two units? Use _SYSTEMD_UNIT=... _PID=... for AND, or put + between match groups for OR.

interview.question: How do you watch a service log?
interview.answer: -f or --follow shows the newest entries and continues printing entries appended to the journal. It stops when Ctrl-C is pressed.
interview.followUp: How can you show kernel messages from the previous boot while using the documented options? Run journalctl -k -b -1.

keyPoints: Use journalctl to read logs stored in the systemd journal.
With no options, it shows the journal entries that the current user can access.
Pass filters to limit the displayed entries.
Structured filters use FIELD=VALUE, such as _SYSTEMD_UNIT=apache.service.
Use -u or --unit to show messages for a systemd unit or matching unit pattern.
Use -b or --boot to select the current boot, another boot, or a boot ID.
gotchas: Do not use -x when attaching output to a bug report. It adds help text that may not be wanted.
The --user option needs persistent journal storage. It may not work when logs exist only in temporary storage.
A file path used as a filter must already exist when journalctl runs.

kill.summary: kill sends a signal to processes or process groups. It sends TERM by default; use KILL only when a process does not stop after TERM.
kill.explanation: The command sends a signal to one or more processes or process groups. Without a signal option, it sends TERM. Use KILL only when TERM does not stop the process, because KILL cannot be caught and gives the process no chance to clean up.

parameters.name: signal
parameters.description: Signal name or number to send; TERM is used when omitted.

parameters.name: PID
parameters.description: Process ID, process-group ID, process name, or supported target form.

kill.returns: Exit status 0 means success, 1 means failure, and 64 means partial success when multiple processes are specified.

example.explanation: First asks the process to stop so it can clean up. If it is still running, the second command forces it to stop.

useCases.title: Stop a process
useCases.scenario: Ask a process to stop cleanly before using a stronger signal.

useCases.title: Check process access
useCases.scenario: Check whether a process can be signaled without sending a real signal.

useCases.title: Use a signal sequence
useCases.scenario: Send escalating signals with delays to the same process.

interview.question: What does kill do when no signal is specified?
interview.answer: It sends the chosen signal to the specified processes or process groups. If no signal is given, it sends TERM, which normally asks the process to exit.
interview.followUp: Why prefer TERM to KILL? TERM lets a process handle the signal and clean up; KILL cannot be caught or handled.

interview.question: When should KILL be used?
interview.answer: TERM is normally preferred because the process can install a handler and exit cleanly. KILL should be a later choice when the process does not stop.
interview.followUp: What happens if the process ignores TERM? Send KILL, but accept that cleanup handlers will not run.

interview.question: How do PID values select targets?
interview.answer: A positive PID targets that process. PID 0 targets processes in the caller's process group, and a negative PID can target a process group.
interview.followUp: How can a command avoid treating a negative process-group ID as an option? Put -- before the negative PID.

keyPoints: kill can signal individual processes or process groups.
The default signal is TERM.
Prefer TERM before KILL so the process can perform cleanup.
gotchas: A timeout sequence can send several signals in order, but each timeout is measured before its next signal.
Signal 0 checks whether the target can be signaled without sending a real signal.
Giving a thread ID still targets the whole process, not one selected thread.
