interview.question: What is less used for?
interview.answer: less displays file or standard-input content in a terminal. It does not need to read the whole input before it starts, so large inputs can appear sooner.
interview.followUp: How can you inspect output from another command? Run the command and pipe it to less, such as `journalctl | less`.

interview.question: How do you search in less?
interview.answer: Press `/`, enter a pattern, and press Enter to search forward. Press `n` to repeat the previous search for the next matching line.
interview.followUp: How can you search without regular-expression meaning? Start the search pattern with Control-R.

interview.question: How do you follow a growing file?
interview.answer: Press `F` to keep reading when the end of a growing file is reached. Interrupt it, usually with Control-C, to stop waiting for more data.
interview.followUp: What is the difference between `F` and `ESC-F`? `ESC-F` also rings the terminal bell when a line matches the last search pattern.

Press `h` or `H` to see the available keyboard commands.
Press Space to move forward by one window. A number before the command changes the count.
Press `g` to go to a line; without a number, it goes to the beginning.
Press `q` to leave the pager.
It can begin displaying large input before reading the complete file.
gotchas: Jumping to a large line number can be slow.
The s command saves input only when the input came from a pipe.
Search patterns are regular expressions by default, so special characters may change the search.

ls.summary: `ls` lists information about files and directories. With no path, it lists the current directory.
ls.explanation: `ls` reads directory entries and prints information about them. Without a path, it uses the current directory. Options change which entries appear, how output is formatted, and how entries are sorted.

parameters.name: OPTION
parameters.description: Options that control displayed entries, formatting, timestamps, and sorting.

parameters.name: FILE
parameters.description: Files or directories to inspect. If omitted, the current directory is used.

ls.returns: Exit status 0 means success, 1 means a minor problem, and 2 means serious trouble.

example.title: List detailed directory contents
example.explanation: Lists all entries, including hidden ones, in long format with readable sizes.

useCases.title: Browse files
useCases.scenario: Inspect the current directory or a named path.

useCases.title: Check metadata
useCases.scenario: See permissions, ownership, sizes, and timestamps.

useCases.title: Sort entries
useCases.scenario: Find the newest or largest entries.

interview.question: What does `ls` do by default?
interview.answer: `ls` lists information about files. With no file argument, it examines the current directory.
interview.followUp: How can you include hidden entries? Use `-a`; it also includes the implied `.` and `..` entries.

interview.question: What does `ls -l` change?
interview.answer: `-l` selects long format. It shows more file metadata than the default name-only format.
interview.followUp: How can sizes be easier to read? Use `-h` together with `-l` or `-s`.

interview.question: How do you list a directory tree and control time sorting?
interview.answer: `-R` lists subdirectories recursively. It continues into nested directories instead of stopping at the named directory.
interview.followUp: How can you sort by newest modification time? Use `-t`; `--time=WORD` selects another timestamp for time display or sorting.

keyPoints: With no path, `ls` examines the current directory. A path or file name limits what it examines.
`-a` includes hidden names that begin with a dot.
`-A` includes hidden names but leaves out the implied current and parent directory entries.
`-l` prints entries in long format with file metadata.
`-R` descends into subdirectories and lists their contents.
`-S` orders entries by size, with the largest first.
`-p` adds a slash after directory names.
gotchas: This is about flatpak remote-ls, not `ls`; do not use it to inspect ordinary directories.
If no sorting option is selected, entries are sorted by name.
A nonzero exit status can indicate an access problem.

lsof.summary: lsof lists files opened by processes. It can inspect ordinary files, directories, devices, and network files, and can emit output for programs to parse.
lsof.explanation: lsof reads information about files opened by processes and writes a listing to standard output. Open files can include regular files, directories, devices, libraries, and network files such as Internet or UNIX sockets.

parameters.name: names
parameters.description: Optional selection names, such as file paths or file-system names, depending on lsof option handling.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: Option and argument string for selecting processes, files, file descriptors, networks, directories, and output behavior.

lsof.returns: Writes file information to standard output. It can also produce output intended for parsing by other programs.

example.title: Find a process listening on TCP port 22
example.explanation: Lists processes with listening TCP sockets on port 22. It keeps addresses and ports numeric.

useCases.title: Investigate file usage
useCases.scenario: Find which process has a file or directory open.

useCases.title: Inspect network files
useCases.scenario: Find processes using a network port or socket.

useCases.title: Search a directory
useCases.scenario: Check open files under a directory.

useCases.title: Process machine-readable output
useCases.scenario: Feed open-file data into a script.

interview.question: What does lsof do?
interview.answer: lsof lists information about files opened by processes. Its scope includes regular files, directories, devices, libraries, and network files such as Internet and UNIX sockets.
interview.followUp: How can output be made easier for another program to parse? Use -F to request machine-oriented output instead of the normal formatted display.

interview.question: How are selection options combined?
interview.answer: Use -a to AND selection options. Without it, selection conditions are generally combined as separate ORed sets before other selection rules are applied.
interview.followUp: How can a command filter by both a process and a network condition? Combine the relevant selectors and add -a when both conditions must match.

interview.question: What is the difference between +d and +D?
interview.answer: Use +d for a top-level directory search and +D for a complete recursive search. The recursive form can be slow because lsof stats every file and directory under the starting path.
interview.followUp: What limits a directory search? Symbolic links and mount points below the directory are not followed or searched unless the appropriate -x option is also used.

keyPoints: The command reports files that processes currently have open.
The meaning of open file is broad. It includes ordinary files, directories, block devices, and character devices.
Network-related objects can appear in the listing, including Internet sockets, NFS files, and UNIX-domain sockets.
Use its machine-readable output mode when a script needs to process results.
The -a option requires selection conditions to match together rather than treating their selection sets independently.
gotchas: Results depend on your permissions. A user may not be able to inspect every file.
Use -b when calls such as stat, lstat, or readlink could block, but the output may be incomplete.

man.summary: man finds and displays system manual pages. It can also search documentation, read a local manual file, or print a page's file location.
man.explanation: man finds and displays system manual pages for programs, utilities, and functions. It can also search page descriptions, search all manual text, work with local files, or print page locations.

parameters.name: section
parameters.description: Optional manual section to search first.

parameters.name: page
parameters.description: Manual page name, such as a command, utility, or function.

parameters.name: regexp or term
parameters.description: Search expression for -k or -K modes.

parameters.name: file
parameters.description: Local nroff source file used with -l.

man.returns: By default, man displays the selected manual page. Search and location modes print matching descriptions or file locations instead.

example.title: Common man commands
example.code:
man ls
man 7 man
man -k printf
man -f smail
man -w ls
example.explanation: These commands display a page, choose section 7, search descriptions, show a short description, and print a source file location.

useCases.title: Read a manual page
useCases.scenario: You need instructions for a command or function.

useCases.title: Search short descriptions
useCases.scenario: You know a topic but not the command name.

useCases.title: Show all section matches
useCases.scenario: You need every matching page in different sections.

useCases.title: Format a local page
useCases.scenario: You want to inspect or process a local manual source file.

interview.question: What does man do?
interview.answer: man normally treats each page argument as the name of a program, utility, or function. It searches the manual collection and displays the first matching page according to the section order.
interview.followUp: How do you select a specific section? Give the section before the page name, such as man 7 man.

interview.question: How can you search for documentation?
interview.answer: Use -k or --apropos to search short manual-page descriptions for a keyword. Use -K or --global-apropos to search text in all manual pages.
interview.followUp: Why can -K be slow? It searches the source of every manual page, so specifying a section can reduce the work.

interview.question: How can you find the file behind a manual page?
interview.answer: Use -w or --where to print the source nroff file location without displaying the page. Use -W to print the location of the preformatted cat file.
interview.followUp: What does -l do? It formats a local manual file instead of searching the system manual collection.

keyPoints: Pass a command, utility, function, or other documented item as the page name.
Add a section number to restrict the lookup, such as man 2 open.
Section 1 documents executable programs and shell commands.
Section 2 documents system calls supplied by the kernel.
Section 3 documents functions provided by program libraries.
Use -f to print a short description for a page when one is available.
gotchas: Without a section number, man searches sections in its configured order and shows only the first matching page.
The global text search normally uses simple strings; regular expressions require the --regex option.
Quote page names containing parentheses so the shell does not interpret them.

mkdir.summary: mkdir creates directories. Use -p for missing parent directories, -m for permissions, and -v for creation messages.
mkdir.explanation: The command creates each directory named on the command line. Without -p, parent directories must already exist. With -p, missing parent directories are created, and an existing directory is accepted. The -m option sets permissions for a new directory, while -v prints a message for each directory created.

parameters.name: OPTION
parameters.description: An option that changes how directories are created.

parameters.name: DIRECTORY
parameters.description: A pathname of a directory to create. More than one directory can be supplied.

mkdir.returns: The page specifies command options and operands but does not state an exit status for this GNU command page.

example.title: Create nested directories
example.explanation: Creates the app directory and then creates its config subdirectory. Existing directories in the path do not cause an error.

useCases.title: Build nested paths
useCases.scenario: Create a directory tree in one command, even when some parent directories are missing.

useCases.title: Set directory permissions
useCases.scenario: Create a new directory with selected permission bits.

useCases.title: Report created directories
useCases.scenario: Show which directories were created during a setup script.

interview.question: What does mkdir -p do?
interview.answer: mkdir creates the directories named by its operands. By default, required parent directories must already exist. The -p option creates missing parents and does not report an error when the target already exists.
interview.followUp: What happens to a parent created with -p when -m is also used? The parent directory's file mode is unaffected by -m.

interview.question: How does mkdir set directory permissions?
interview.answer: The -m option sets the mode of each newly created directory using chmod-style mode syntax. Without -m, the normal directory mode is modified by the process umask.
interview.followUp: Can -m change an existing directory? No. mkdir creates directories; an existing directory is ignored only when -p is used.

interview.question: What are the main mkdir options?
interview.answer: The command accepts one or more directory operands. Useful options include -m or --mode for permissions, -p or --parents for missing parents, and -v or --verbose for creation messages.
interview.followUp: How can you set an SELinux or SMACK context? Use -Z for the default type or --context with an explicit context.

keyPoints: mkdir creates one or more directories that do not already exist.
Use -m or --mode to choose permissions for a newly created directory.
Use -p or --parents to create missing parent directories and accept an existing directory without an error.
Use -v or --verbose to report each directory that the command creates.
Use -Z to assign the default SELinux security context to each created directory.
Use --context with a value to assign a specified SELinux or SMACK context.
gotchas: The final permissions are affected by the process umask when you use the normal creation behavior. A mode passed with -m uses chmod-style syntax.
Use -p when the path may already exist or when parent directories are missing. The -m option does not change the modes of parent directories created by -p.

mv.summary: `mv` moves or renames files, directories, and symbolic links. It can also control overwrites, backups, updates, and output.
mv.explanation: `mv` changes a file, directory, or symbolic link to a new name or location. With several sources, the final operand must be an existing directory, or use `-t` to name the target directory.
mv.syntax:
mv [OPTION]... [-T] SOURCE DEST
mv [OPTION]... SOURCE ... DIRECTORY
mv [OPTION]... -t DIRECTORY SOURCE ...

parameters.name: SOURCE
parameters.description: One source path to rename or move.

parameters.name: DEST
parameters.description: A new path, or the destination directory when several sources are given.

parameters.name: DIRECTORY
parameters.description: An existing directory that receives all source paths.

mv.returns: The command returns status 0 when all input files are moved successfully. A value greater than 0 means an error occurred.

example.title: Move and rename files
example.code:
mv report.txt archive/report.txt
mv -i old.txt new.txt
mv -v src.txt backup/
example.explanation: The first command renames or moves a file. The second asks before replacing an existing destination. The third prints each move.

useCases.title: Rename an item
useCases.scenario: Change a file or directory name without changing its parent directory.

useCases.title: Move multiple sources
useCases.scenario: Place several files into an existing directory.

useCases.title: Update selected files
useCases.scenario: Avoid replacing newer destination files during an update.

useCases.title: Show move details
useCases.scenario: See each operation while a script or command runs.

interview.question: What are the main forms of `mv`?
interview.answer: `mv SOURCE DEST` renames one source or moves it to a destination. If the final operand is an existing directory, each source is placed inside it.
interview.followUp: How can you force the multi-source form? Use `-t DIRECTORY` and provide the sources after it.

interview.question: How does `mv` control overwriting?
interview.answer: `-i` asks before overwriting, `-f` does not ask, and `-n` avoids overwriting. If more than one is supplied, the final one wins.
interview.followUp: What happens with `mv -i -f source dest`? `-f` wins because it appears last.

interview.question: What happens across file systems?
interview.answer: On the same file system, `mv` can use a rename operation. If that fails because the locations are on different file systems, it copies the source and then removes the original.
interview.followUp: What risk does this fallback have? An interruption can leave a partial copy at the source or destination.

keyPoints: Use `mv` to rename one item or move one or more items into a directory.
Use `-t DIRECTORY` when you want to state the destination directory before listing the sources.
Use `-T` to prevent the destination from being treated as a directory.
Use `-v` to print what each move does.
Use `--backup` when existing destination files should receive backups before replacement.
Use `--update` to choose which existing destination files may be replaced, including only older ones.
Use `-Z` to set the destination file's SELinux context to its default type.
gotchas: When combining `-i`, `-f`, and `-n`, only the last option controls overwrite behavior.
`git mv` updates Git's index, but you still need a commit to save the change in the repository.
A cross-file-system move can leave a partial copy if copying or removal stops because of an error or signal.

Namespaces.summary: Linux namespaces isolate global resources for selected processes. They support separate views of networking, processes, mounts, users, hostnames, clocks, IPC, and cgroup roots.
Namespaces.explanation: A Linux namespace gives processes an isolated view of one global resource. Different namespace types isolate items such as process IDs, network devices, mount points, user IDs, hostnames, clocks, or cgroup roots. Processes can create namespaces, enter existing ones, or move themselves into new ones.

parameters.name: flags
parameters.description: Flags selecting namespace types, such as CLONE_NEWNET or CLONE_NEWUSER.

parameters.name: namespace file descriptor
parameters.description: A file descriptor referring to a namespace file, usually under /proc/PID/ns.

Namespaces.returns: The namespace operations report success or failure through their system-call return values; the page specifically notes ENOSPC for namespace creation after configured limits are reached.

example.title: Create user and network namespaces
example.explanation: This starts a shell with new user and network namespaces. The shell can have its own network view, but network setup may need extra commands and permissions.

useCases.title: Build container isolation
useCases.scenario: Run a group of processes with its own process, mount, user, or network view.

useCases.title: Inspect a running process
useCases.scenario: Enter another process's namespaces for inspection or administration.

useCases.title: Separate network environments
useCases.scenario: Give a service an isolated network stack and connect it with veth devices.

interview.question: What does a Linux namespace provide?
interview.answer: A namespace isolates a global resource so processes inside see their own instance. Changes are visible to processes in that namespace but hidden from processes in other namespaces.
interview.followUp: How can a namespace remain after its processes exit? An open or bind-mounted /proc/PID/ns file can hold it alive; hierarchy and related mounts can also pin it.

interview.question: How are namespaces created and entered?
interview.answer: clone() can create a child in new namespaces when given CLONE_NEW* flags. unshare() creates namespaces and moves the calling process into them, while setns() joins an existing namespace through a namespace file descriptor.
interview.followUp: What privilege is normally needed? Most clone() and unshare() namespace creation needs CAP_SYS_ADMIN, but creating a user namespace needs no privilege since Linux 3.8.

interview.question: What does a network namespace isolate?
interview.answer: Network namespaces isolate network devices, protocol stacks, routes, firewall rules, ports, and related proc and sysfs views. A physical device belongs to one network namespace, and a veth pair can connect namespaces.
interview.followUp: What happens to a physical device when its namespace ends? The kernel moves it back to the initial network namespace, while veth devices in the ended namespace are destroyed.

keyPoints: A namespace makes a shared system resource look like a separate resource to its member processes.
Use setns() to enter an existing namespace through a file descriptor.
Use unshare() to create selected namespaces and move the caller into them.
The /proc/PID/ns directory exposes handles for the process's namespaces.
A physical network device cannot belong to more than one network namespace at a time.
gotchas: A namespace normally ends when its last process leaves or terminates. Open namespace file descriptors and bind mounts can keep it alive.
Most namespace creation needs CAP_SYS_ADMIN. User namespaces are the main exception.
Virtual Ethernet devices inside a network namespace are destroyed when that namespace ends.

PATH.summary: The exec family replaces the current process image with another program. Different forms choose how to pass arguments, the environment, and whether to search PATH.
PATH.explanation: The exec functions replace the calling process with another program. The l forms receive arguments one by one, while the v forms receive an argument array. Functions ending in p search PATH when the file name has no slash. Functions ending in e use the supplied environment array.

parameters.name: path
parameters.description: Pathname of the program to execute; used by the non-p forms.

parameters.name: file
parameters.description: File name to find through PATH when it has no slash; used by the p forms.

parameters.name: arg, ...
parameters.description: First argument and following arguments as separate strings; terminate with (char *) NULL.

parameters.name: argv
parameters.description: Array of argument strings terminated by a null pointer.

parameters.name: envp
parameters.description: Environment array for the new process image.

PATH.returns: On failure, returns -1 and sets errno. On success, it does not return.

example.title: PATH lookup
example.code:
# Run a program found through PATH
/bin/echo "hello"
example.explanation: This shell example shows the kind of program lookup that the p-suffixed exec functions perform. It is runnable, but it does not call the C library functions directly.

useCases.title: Replace the current program
useCases.scenario: Start another program from a process.

useCases.title: Pass command-line arguments
useCases.scenario: Give a program arguments as separate values or an array.

useCases.title: Set the child environment
useCases.scenario: Use a controlled environment for the new program.

useCases.title: Run by command name
useCases.scenario: Find an executable using PATH.

interview.question: What is the difference between the l and v forms?
interview.answer: The l forms take arguments as separate values, while the v forms take an array of argument pointers. The first argument normally names the executed file, and the argument list ends with a null pointer.
interview.followUp: How would you pass a custom environment? Use execle or execvpe, which accept an environment array. Remember that execvpe still searches using PATH from the caller's environment.

interview.question: When do the p forms search PATH?
interview.answer: The p forms search the colon-separated PATH when the file name has no slash. If the name contains a slash, PATH is ignored and that pathname is used.
interview.followUp: What happens after a permission error during PATH search? The function continues searching, but returns EACCES if no later file works.

interview.question: What does exec return on success or failure?
interview.answer: The exec functions return -1 and set errno when they cannot replace the process image. On success, they do not return because the current process has become the new program.
interview.followUp: What does execlp do for an unrecognized executable header? It runs /bin/sh with the file path as its first argument, unless that shell attempt fails.

keyPoints: An exec call keeps the process but replaces the program image.
Without e in the name, the new program receives the calling process's environ.
The p forms imitate shell-style executable lookup when the name has no slash.
A slash in the file name disables PATH search for p forms.
For an unrecognized file header, p forms try /bin/sh with the file path.
gotchas: The l forms need a final null pointer, and variadic calls should cast it to char *.
A successful call does not return. Code after the call runs only when execution failed.

ping.summary: ping sends ICMP Echo Requests to a host and waits for Echo Replies. It reports reachability, packet loss, and round-trip timing for IPv4 or IPv6.
ping.explanation: ping sends ICMP Echo Request packets to a host and waits for Echo Reply packets. It supports IPv4 and IPv6, measures round-trip time, and reports packet loss after the probes finish.

parameters.name: count
parameters.description: Number of Echo Reply packets to receive before stopping.

parameters.name: interval
parameters.description: Seconds between packets; decimal values are allowed.

parameters.name: deadline
parameters.description: Seconds to wait before exiting regardless of probe progress.

parameters.name: timeout
parameters.description: Seconds to wait for a response when no response has arrived.

parameters.name: packetsize
parameters.description: Number of data bytes in each packet.

parameters.name: destination
parameters.description: Destination host or address to test.

ping.returns: Exit code 0 means success. Exit code 1 means no replies, or too few replies before a specified deadline. Exit code 2 means another error.

example.title: Send four probes
example.explanation: Sends four ICMP echo requests and then prints a summary of the replies.

useCases.title: Find where connectivity fails
useCases.scenario: Check whether a local interface and nearby gateway respond before testing more distant hosts.

useCases.title: Check network quality
useCases.scenario: Measure packet loss and response-time variation between a machine and a host.

useCases.title: Test an IPv6 link-local address
useCases.scenario: Test IPv6 link-local reachability by naming the required interface.

interview.question: How does ping test network reachability?
interview.answer: ping sends ICMP Echo Requests and measures the time until Echo Replies arrive. It uses these results to calculate packet loss and round-trip statistics.
interview.followUp: What does a nonzero mdev indicate? A larger population standard deviation means the round-trip time varies more, which can hurt bulk transfers and VoIP quality.

interview.question: How do -c and -w differ?
interview.answer: With -c, ping stops after the requested number of probes when the replies are complete. With -w, it also has an overall deadline and can stop before receiving all requested replies.
interview.followUp: What happens when both are used? Exit code 1 is returned if fewer than count replies arrive before the deadline.

interview.question: What do ping's exit codes mean?
interview.answer: Exit code 0 means the operation succeeded. Exit code 1 means no replies arrived, or the deadline ended before the required replies; exit code 2 means another error occurred.
interview.followUp: Can a successful exit code prove an application works? No. It only shows that the ICMP test succeeded, not that a particular service accepts traffic.

keyPoints: The command tests a host by sending ICMP Echo Requests and waiting for Echo Replies.
Use -4 or -6 to force one IP version.
The final report includes response timing and the percentage of lost packets.
Duplicate replies are reported and are excluded from packet-loss calculations.
Without -i, normal mode waits one second between probes.
The default payload size is 56 data bytes; the ICMP header makes the packet data total 64 bytes.
The -t option sets IPv4 TTL, which limits how many routers a packet can cross.
gotchas: A failed reachability test returns exit code 1, while other errors return 2.
IPv6 link-local addresses need an output interface, such as a % interface suffix or -I.
Very short intervals require elevated privileges.

Pipes.summary: A Linux pipe is a one-way byte stream between processes. pipe() returns separate file descriptors for reading and writing; reads and writes normally wait when the pipe cannot proceed.
Pipes.explanation: A pipe is a one-way byte stream with separate read and write ends. The pipe(2) call returns two file descriptors. A read from an empty pipe waits for data, while a write to a full pipe waits for space. After fork(), related processes can close unused ends and communicate through the remaining descriptors.

parameters.name: fildes[2]
parameters.description: Two-element array filled with descriptors for the read and write ends; element 0 is the read end and element 1 is the write end.

parameters.name: pipe
parameters.description: The pipe(2) page defines no function arguments beyond the descriptor array; this card uses the POSIX declaration.

Pipes.returns: On success, pipe() returns 0 and fills both descriptors. On failure, it returns -1 and sets errno.

example.title: Send data through a pipe
example.code:
import os

read_fd, write_fd = os.pipe()
os.write(write_fd, b"Hello\n")
os.close(write_fd)
print(os.read(read_fd, 100).decode(), end="")
os.close(read_fd)
example.explanation: This creates a pipe, writes bytes to its write end, reads them from its read end, and closes both descriptors.

useCases.title: Parent-child communication
useCases.scenario: A parent creates a pipe, forks, and sends data to its child.

useCases.title: Command pipelines
useCases.scenario: A shell connects one command's output to another command's input.

useCases.title: Local process data transfer
useCases.scenario: A process sends a byte stream to another process without creating a filesystem name.

interview.question: What does pipe() return?
interview.answer: pipe() creates a pipe and returns two file descriptors: index 0 is the read end and index 1 is the write end. Data written to one end can be read from the other.
interview.followUp: How should a parent and child use the descriptors after fork()? Each process should close the end it does not use before transferring data.

interview.question: When do pipe reads and writes block?
interview.answer: A blocking read waits when the pipe is empty. A blocking write waits when the pipe is full. O_NONBLOCK changes these operations so they return instead of waiting when they cannot proceed.
interview.followUp: What happens with a nonblocking read and no possible writers? It succeeds and returns an empty result; with writers still present, it fails with EAGAIN.

interview.question: Does a pipe preserve write boundaries?
interview.answer: A pipe is a byte stream, so it has no message boundaries. For reliable records, the application must define its own framing and handle partial reads and writes.
interview.followUp: Can separate writes be interleaved? Yes. Writes larger than PIPE_BUF may be interleaved with writes from other processes.

keyPoints: A pipe carries data in one direction between processes.
pipe() returns one descriptor for reading and one for writing.
A normal read waits until data arrives when the pipe is empty.
A normal write waits for free capacity when the pipe is full.
Pipes and FIFOs have the same I/O behavior after they are created and opened.
POSIX pipe() starts with O_NONBLOCK and FD_CLOEXEC cleared on both descriptors.
gotchas: A pipe does not preserve message boundaries. One read may receive only part of a write, or data from multiple writes.
A reader sees end-of-file only after every descriptor for the write end has been closed.
Linux pipes are unidirectional. Portable programs should not assume that one pipe supports two-way communication.

Processes.summary: ps displays a snapshot of selected active processes. It can select processes and control which fields are shown.
Processes.explanation: The ps command reads process information from the virtual /proc filesystem and prints a selected view. You can choose processes by process ID, command name, user, group, session, or terminal, then choose output fields and sort the result.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: Option list and arguments that select processes and control output.

parameters.name: pidlist
parameters.description: One or more process IDs for PID selection.

parameters.name: format/spec
parameters.description: One or more output fields and optional sort directions.

Processes.returns: A formatted snapshot of the selected processes is written to standard output.

example.title: Show one process
example.explanation: This prints the process ID, executable name, and command-line arguments for one process.

useCases.title: Inspect a process
useCases.scenario: Find the ID and command of a running program.

useCases.title: Create a process report
useCases.scenario: List every process with selected fields.

useCases.title: Order process output
useCases.scenario: Sort processes by a resource or identifier.

interview.question: What does ps do by default?
interview.answer: ps reports a snapshot of selected active processes. By default, it shows processes owned by the current effective user and attached to the same terminal.
interview.followUp: How can you inspect every process? Use ps -e or ps -A; both select all processes.

interview.question: How do you select processes?
interview.answer: Use -p with a process ID list, such as ps -p 42. Use -C with a command-name list when selection should use the executable name.
interview.followUp: What is different about -q? Quick PID mode reads only the listed PIDs, keeps their order, and does not allow extra selection or sorting.

interview.question: How do you control ps output?
interview.answer: Use -o or --format with format specifiers to choose columns, and use --sort to set the order. For example, ps -eo pid,comm --sort=-pcpu selects fields and sorts by CPU use.
interview.followUp: Why might command arguments be missing? The comm field is the executable name, while args is the command line; choose args when arguments are needed.

keyPoints: ps gives a point-in-time view of processes; use top when you need repeated updates.
The -p option selects processes whose process IDs are in the supplied list.
The -C option selects processes by executable name, not by the complete command line.
The -f option requests a full-format listing and also prints command arguments.
The --sort option accepts one or more format keys, with optional plus or minus direction markers.
This implementation obtains process details from /proc and does not need special privileges.
gotchas: Do not treat ps -aux and ps aux as equivalent. They use different option styles and can select different processes.
The default output order is not sorted. Add a sorting option when order matters.
Avoid ps -aux in scripts. Use a clear option form such as ps aux or ps -e.

ps.summary: ps reports a snapshot of selected active processes. It can filter processes and choose the columns shown.
ps.explanation: ps takes a snapshot of selected active processes and prints information about them. You can select processes by IDs, users, terminals, or commands, then choose the output columns and sort order.

parameters.name: option
parameters.description: Option and its argument, such as -p 123 or -o pid,comm.

ps.returns: On success, ps exits with status 0. A value greater than 0 means an error occurred.

example.explanation: Lists processes with selected columns and puts the highest CPU users first.

useCases.title: System process listing
useCases.scenario: Inspect all processes and their standard details.

useCases.title: Process lookup
useCases.scenario: Find a process by executable name or PID.

useCases.title: Custom reports
useCases.scenario: Create stable, script-friendly columns.

useCases.title: Process tree
useCases.scenario: View parent-child relationships.

interview.question: What does ps show by default?
interview.answer: By default, ps shows processes with the caller's effective user ID that use the caller's terminal. It prints fields such as PID, terminal, CPU time, and executable name.
interview.followUp: How can you list every process? Use -A or -e; these options are equivalent.

interview.question: How do you select specific processes?
interview.answer: Use selection options such as -p for process IDs, -u for effective users, -U for real users, -t for terminals, and -C for executable names. When selection options are supplied, their criteria are combined inclusively.
interview.followUp: What happens when several selection options are used? A process is selected if it matches any supplied criterion, because the selections are additive.

interview.question: How do you control ps output columns?
interview.answer: Use -o with a comma-separated or space-separated list of format keywords, such as -o pid,ppid,comm. You can rename headers with an equals sign, and empty all headers to suppress the header line.
interview.followUp: How do you control a column's width? Use a width suffix such as wchan:42 in a format specification.

keyPoints: ps reports information about a chosen set of active processes.
Unix-style options use a leading dash and can be grouped.
Use -e or -A to select every process on the system.
Use -p with a list of PIDs to select processes by process ID.
Use -C with command names to select processes by executable name.
Use -o to choose and order the output columns yourself.
gotchas: Do not assume the default output is sorted. Add an explicit sort option when order matters.
Selecting with -C matches the executable name, not the complete command line and its arguments.
The output is a point-in-time snapshot. A process can change or exit before you read the result.

pwd.summary: pwd prints the absolute path of the current working directory. Use -L for the logical PWD path or -P to resolve symbolic links; the GNU utility uses -P by default.
pwd.explanation: The command writes the absolute path of the current working directory. Logical mode can use the shell's PWD value, which may keep symbolic-link components. Physical mode resolves symbolic links. The documented utility defaults to physical mode, while POSIX specifies logical behavior when no option is given.

parameters.name: -L, --logical
parameters.description: Select the logical path, using PWD when valid; it may contain symbolic links.

parameters.name: -P, --physical
parameters.description: Select the physical path by resolving symbolic links.

parameters.name: --help
parameters.description: Show help and exit.

parameters.name: --version
parameters.description: Show version information and exit.

pwd.returns: Writes the absolute current-working-directory path to standard output. The GNU utility returns 0 unless an error occurs while reading the directory name or an invalid option is supplied; errors return a nonzero status.

example.title: Print the current directory
example.explanation: Run these commands in a shell to print the current directory using the default, logical, and physical forms.

useCases.scenario: Check where a shell or script is operating before running file commands.

useCases.title: Show the logical path
useCases.scenario: Keep a path that follows a symbolic-link location.

useCases.title: Show the physical path
useCases.scenario: Get a canonical directory path without symbolic links.

useCases.title: Use the path in automation
useCases.scenario: Pass the current directory to another command or script.

interview.question: What does pwd do?
interview.answer: pwd prints the absolute pathname of the current working directory. With -P, symbolic links are resolved; with -L, the path may retain symbolic links through the PWD value.
interview.followUp: How does the default differ between the documented sources? GNU pwd assumes -P when no option is given, while POSIX requires behavior as if -L was used.

interview.question: When should -L be used?
interview.answer: The -L option uses the PWD environment value when it is an absolute path for the current directory. The result can therefore contain symbolic-link components.
interview.followUp: What if PWD is invalid? POSIX says -L then behaves like -P, so the physical directory path is used.

interview.question: How can a script detect failure?
interview.answer: A successful command returns status 0. An error, such as an invalid option or failure while reading the directory name, returns a nonzero status and produces no normal output.
interview.followUp: Where are diagnostics written? They go to standard error, while the directory path goes to standard output.

keyPoints: pwd prints the complete path of the directory in which the shell is currently operating.
Use -L when you want the logical path recorded in the PWD environment variable.
Use -P to remove symbolic-link components and show the physical directory path.
For the GNU utility page, omitting an option selects physical mode.
The output is an absolute path, not a path relative to the current location.
The command writes one directory path followed by a newline.
gotchas: A shell may run its built-in pwd instead of the external utility. Its supported options and default behavior can differ.
When both POSIX options appear, the final one controls the result.

Redirection.summary: Bash redirection controls command file descriptors. It can connect input and output to files or pipes, copy descriptors, and close them. The exec builtin applies descriptor changes to the current shell or replaces the shell with a command.
Redirection.explanation: Bash applies redirections while setting up a command. A redirection can connect standard input or output to a file, duplicate or close a file descriptor, or change the descriptors in the current shell when used with exec. The POSIX exec utility can also replace the shell process with another command.

parameters.name: command
parameters.description: Optional command to run. With exec, it replaces the shell process.

parameters.name: argument ...
parameters.description: Arguments passed to command.

parameters.name: redirection
parameters.description: A file descriptor and redirection operator, such as 3<file or 3<&-.

Redirection.returns: With a command, exec does not return to the shell after replacement. If the command is not found, the status is 127; if it is not executable, 126. Without a command, a successful exec redirection returns zero; a redirection error makes the shell exit with a status from 1 through 125.

example.explanation: This opens input.txt on file descriptor 3, reads from it with cat, then closes descriptor 3.

useCases.title: Manage a persistent input or output descriptor
useCases.scenario: Keep a file open and reuse it across several commands.

useCases.title: Combine pipeline output

useCases.title: Replace the current shell
useCases.scenario: Start another program without keeping the shell process.

useCases.title: Use custom file descriptors
useCases.scenario: Pass a chosen input or output descriptor to a command.

interview.question: What does shell redirection do?
interview.answer: Bash redirection changes where a command reads or writes. It can open files, duplicate descriptors, or close descriptors. With exec and no command, the change applies to the current shell.
interview.followUp: What does exec command do? It replaces the shell with command without creating a new process, so the shell does not return after a successful replacement.

interview.question: How can a script manage extra file descriptors?
interview.answer: The usual descriptors are 0 for standard input, 1 for standard output, and 2 for standard error. Syntax such as 3<file opens file descriptor 3 for reading, while 5<&0 copies descriptor 0 to descriptor 5.
interview.followUp: How do you close descriptor 3? Use exec 3<&-; the POSIX page gives this form for closing a descriptor.

interview.question: How do pipelines interact with redirection?
interview.answer: The pipeline operator | connects one command's standard output to the next command's standard input. The |& form also sends the first command's standard error through the pipe, equivalent to 2>&1 |.
interview.followUp: What determines a pipeline's status? Normally it is the last command's status; with pipefail, it is the rightmost non-zero status, or zero if all commands succeed.

keyPoints: Quoting matters in redirection syntax. A backslash can remove the special meaning of the next character, so quote characters when they should be treated literally.
The | operator sends the first command's standard output to the second command's standard input.
The |& operator sends both standard output and standard error from the first command through the pipe.
Use exec with a numbered descriptor to keep a file open in the current shell for later commands.
A descriptor can be duplicated from another descriptor with the <& form.
gotchas: Using exec with only a redirection changes the current shell. The descriptor can remain open for later commands, so close it explicitly when it is no longer needed.
For a pipeline, the pipe connection is made before command1's own redirections. Do not assume a later redirection changes both sides of the pipe.

rm.summary: `rm` removes named files. Use `-r` for directories and their contents, and use interactive options when you want confirmation.
rm.explanation: `rm` removes the files named on the command line. It does not remove directories unless a directory option is used. Recursive mode removes a directory and the entries inside it; interactive options can ask for confirmation.

parameters.name: OPTION
parameters.description: Options that control prompting, recursion, safety, output, and file-system handling.

parameters.name: FILE
parameters.description: Files or directories to remove.

rm.returns: The command returns a nonzero status when an error occurs. Under POSIX, status 0 means all directory entries were removed or removal was canceled by a negative confirmation.

example.explanation: Removes the build directory and asks before each removal.

useCases.scenario: Remove one or more files that are no longer needed.

useCases.title: Delete a directory recursively

useCases.title: Review removals
useCases.scenario: Use confirmation prompts before destructive operations.

interview.question: What does `rm` do by default?
interview.answer: `rm` removes each named file. It does not remove directories by default, and `-r` removes directories together with their contents.
interview.followUp: How can you reduce accidental removal? Use `-i` for every removal or `-I` for a single confirmation before a large operation.

interview.question: How do the interactive options differ?
interview.answer: `-f` ignores missing files and does not prompt. `-i` prompts before every removal. When both are used, the page says `-f` does not prevent the `-i` behavior in the GNU option description?
interview.followUp: Which option is less intrusive for large operations? `-I` prompts once when removing more than three files or when removing recursively.

interview.question: How can recursive removal avoid crossing file systems?
interview.answer: With recursive removal, `--one-file-system` skips directories on a different file system from the command-line argument's file system.
interview.followUp: What does `--preserve-root=all` add? It rejects command-line arguments on a separate device from their parent.

keyPoints: The command removes every file named in its arguments.
`-f` ignores missing paths and prevents prompts.
`-i` asks for confirmation before each removal.
`-r`, `-R`, and `--recursive` remove directory trees.
`-d` removes empty directories.
gotchas: A directory is not removed unless you use a directory option such as `-r` or `-d`.
`--no-preserve-root` disables the special protection for `/`; use it only when you fully understand the result.

rsync.summary: rsync copies files locally or between hosts. It finds changed files and can send only changed data while preserving selected file attributes.
rsync.explanation: rsync compares source and destination files using size and modification time by default. It transfers changed data and can preserve links, permissions, ownership, and other attributes. It works locally, through a remote shell such as SSH, or through an rsync daemon.

parameters.description: One or more local or remote source paths.

parameters.name: DEST
parameters.description: Optional local or remote destination path. If omitted with one source, rsync lists files.

rsync.returns: Copies or lists files. With one source and no destination, it lists the source files instead of copying.

useCases.title: Remote-shell transfer
useCases.scenario: Copy changed files to or from a host over SSH or another remote shell.

useCases.title: Daemon transfer
useCases.scenario: Mirror or retrieve files exposed by an rsync daemon.

useCases.title: Incremental backup

interview.question: Which transfer methods does rsync support?
interview.answer: rsync can copy files locally, through a remote shell, or through an rsync daemon. A single colon after a host selects the remote-shell form. A double colon or an rsync URL selects daemon access.
interview.followUp: How can a command list a remote source instead of copying it? Use one source argument without a destination; rsync lists the matching files.

interview.question: How does rsync decide what to transfer?
interview.answer: The default quick check looks for a changed file size or modification time. When data needs updating, rsync uses its delta-transfer protocol to send differences instead of the whole file.
interview.followUp: What happens when file data is unchanged but requested attributes differ? rsync can update those destination attributes directly.

interview.question: What does archive mode do?
interview.answer: Archive mode is enabled with `-a`. It recursively copies and preserves attributes such as symbolic links, permissions, ownership, and groups, subject to the permissions and platform support available.
interview.followUp: How do you copy only directory contents rather than adding the source directory level? Add a trailing slash to the source path.

keyPoints: The delta-transfer algorithm sends only changed data, which can reduce network traffic.
Options can preserve links, devices, owners, groups, and permissions.
A local copy uses source and destination paths without a host separator.
Use one colon after a host for a remote-shell transfer, commonly with SSH.
Use two colons or an rsync URL to connect directly to an rsync daemon.
Rsync may transfer command-line items in sorted order rather than the order supplied.
gotchas: A trailing slash changes directory behavior. Without it, the directory name is normally created below the destination. With it, rsync copies the directory contents there.
For remote-shell transfers, install rsync on both machines.

scp.summary: scp copies files between local and remote hosts over SSH. It uses SFTP by default and accepts local paths, remote host paths, or scp URIs.
scp.explanation: scp opens an SSH connection and transfers files with SFTP by default. The source and target can be local paths, remote paths in the form [user@]host:[path], or scp URIs. It uses SSH authentication, so it can request a password or passphrase when needed.
scp.syntax: scp [ -346ABCOpqRrsTv ] [ -c cipher ] [ -D sftp_server_path ] [ -F ssh_config ] [ -i identity_file ] [ -J destination ] [ -l limit ] [ -o ssh_option ] [ -P port ] [ -S program ] [ -X sftp_option ] source ... target

interview.question: How does scp transfer files securely?
interview.answer: scp copies files between hosts over an SSH connection. Current OpenSSH versions use SFTP for the transfer by default, while SSH supplies authentication and security.
interview.followUp: How would you use the older protocol? Use -O, which forces the legacy SCP protocol; this may help with servers without SFTP support or older path and wildcard behavior.

interview.question: How do you copy a directory?
interview.answer: Use -r to copy a directory and its contents recursively. The command follows symbolic links it encounters during traversal.
interview.followUp: What should you check before using -r? Check whether links in the directory tree should be followed, because linked files or directories may be copied unexpectedly.

interview.question: What does -3 do?
interview.answer: Use -3 when two remote hosts should transfer through the local host. Without -3, scp copies directly between the remote hosts.
interview.followUp: What limitation applies to remote authentication in this mode with legacy SCP? With -O, -3 uses batch mode for the second host because scp cannot request credentials for both hosts.

keyPoints: scp copies files between computers on a network.
Transfers use SFTP over SSH by default.
A source or target can be a local path.
Remote locations can use an scp URI with an optional user, port, and path.
Use capital -P to select the remote SSH port.
Use -p to preserve source timestamps and permission bits.
An exit status of zero means success; a value above zero means an error.
gotchas: With -r, scp follows symbolic links while walking the directory tree.
With -R, the origin host must log in to the destination without a password prompt.
Filename wildcard behavior can make strict checking reject files you intended to copy.

sed.summary: sed is a stream editor for filtering and transforming text. It reads files or standard input, applies a script, and writes the result to standard output.
sed.explanation: sed reads text one line at a time into its pattern space, applies selected script commands, and normally writes the resulting pattern space. It can read files or standard input, and commands can select lines by numbers, regular expressions, or ranges.

interview.question: What is sed used for?
interview.answer: sed is a stream editor for basic text transformations. It reads an input stream, applies scripted commands in one pass, and is useful in pipelines.
interview.followUp: How does sed normally output data? It automatically prints the pattern space at the end of each cycle unless -n suppresses that behavior.

interview.question: What are the pattern space and hold space?
interview.answer: The pattern space holds the current input text being processed. The hold space stores text so commands can save it, retrieve it, append to it, or exchange it with the pattern space.
interview.followUp: Which commands exchange these spaces? h and H copy or append the pattern space to hold space; g and G copy or append in the other direction; x exchanges them.

interview.question: How do sed addresses work?
interview.answer: An address selects which input lines receive a command. It can be a line number, the last line, a regular expression, or a two-address inclusive range.
interview.followUp: What does ! do after an address? It reverses selection, so the command runs only when the address or range does not match.

keyPoints: sed transforms text from a file or pipeline.
With no input file, sed reads standard input.
Use -n when output should appear only from explicit print commands.
Use -e to provide a script. Multiple expressions can build one command sequence.
Use -E for extended regular expressions.
The d command discards the current pattern space and starts processing the next input cycle.
The s command replaces text matched by a regular expression.
gotchas: Without -e or -f, sed treats the first non-option argument as the script. Later arguments are input files.
A two-address command includes the whole selected range, including both matching endpoints.
In-place editing changes files directly. Add a suffix if a backup copy is needed.

SHELL.explanation: su authenticates and starts a shell or command with another user and group identity. With --login, it clears most environment variables, sets login variables, changes to the target home directory, and starts the shell as a login shell.

interview.question: What does su do?
interview.answer: su runs a shell or command with a substitute user and group ID. If no user is given, it uses root; extra arguments are passed to the shell.
interview.followUp: How should a privileged script usually switch users? Use runuser when authentication is not needed; use setpriv if no PAM session is needed.

interview.question: What does --login change?
interview.answer: --login creates a login-like environment. It clears most variables, initializes login variables and PATH, changes to the target user's home directory, and marks the shell as a login shell.
interview.followUp: Does --preserve-environment override --login? No. The page says --preserve-environment is ignored when --login is used.

interview.question: Why use --pty?
interview.answer: --pty creates a separate pseudoterminal and makes su proxy input and output between the sessions. This prevents the target session from sharing the original terminal.
interview.followUp: When might --pty be less useful? It is mainly designed for interactive sessions, and piped input disables terminal echo to avoid messy output.

If you omit the user, su starts an interactive root shell.
By default, su keeps the current directory and changes only a limited set of environment variables.
Use -c or --command to pass one command string to the target shell.
Use --pty for a separate terminal connection, especially for interactive sessions.
--session-command runs a command without creating a new session, but the page discourages this option.

A requested shell can be ignored for a target user with a restricted shell unless the caller is root.
For privileged scripts, the page recommends runuser instead because it does not require authentication.

interview.question: What does sh do?
interview.answer: sh is a standard command language interpreter. It can read commands from a file, from a string passed with -c, or from standard input with -s.
interview.followUp: How can a script provide positional arguments when using -c? The command name and following arguments are supplied after the command string.

interview.question: What are the main ways to provide commands to sh?
interview.answer: The first form runs commands from command_file. The -c form runs command_string, and the -s form reads commands from standard input.
interview.followUp: When is -s useful? It is useful when commands are supplied through a pipe or another standard-input source.

interview.question: How are sh options represented?
interview.answer: Options can be written with a leading - or +, and the synopsis includes short options such as -e, -n, -u, and -x, plus the -o option form.
interview.followUp: Why should option behavior be checked for a particular shell? POSIX defines the interface, but the Linux implementation may have differences.

The command accepts several short options and repeated -o option settings.
Without -c or -s, sh can read commands from a command file and receive arguments.
With -c, sh executes one command string and can assign a command name and arguments.
With -s, sh reads commands from standard input.
gotchas: This page describes POSIX sh. Linux shell behavior can differ, so check the implementation-specific documentation when portability matters.

sort.summary: sort orders lines from files or standard input and writes the result. Options control comparisons, fields, output, checking, merging, and duplicate handling.
sort.explanation: sort reads lines from the named files, or from standard input when no file is given or a file name is -. It compares each line using the selected ordering rules and writes the combined sorted text to standard output.

interview.question: What does sort do by default?
interview.answer: sort combines input lines and writes them in comparison order. With no input file, or with -, it reads standard input.
interview.followUp: How can you sort numeric values? Use -n for string numeric values, -g for general numeric values, or -h for human-readable values such as 2K and 1G.

interview.question: How do you sort by a field?
interview.answer: Use -t to choose a field separator and provide a key such as -k2,2. A key can specify a field and an optional character position, and key-specific ordering letters can override global options.
interview.followUp: How would you sort by the second field numerically and keep equal keys in input order? Use sort -t, -k2,2n -s.

interview.question: How can sort validate sorted input?
interview.answer: The -c option checks whether input is sorted and reports the first bad line. The -C option performs the same check but stays quiet; both avoid sorting the input.
interview.followUp: What does -u add when checking? With -c, it checks for strict ordering rather than allowing equal keys.

keyPoints: Multiple input files are treated as one combined stream, and the sorted result goes to standard output unless -o is used.
Use -b when spaces at the start of a line should not affect key comparisons.
Use -d for dictionary order, which ignores characters other than blanks and letters or digits.
Use -V when text contains version-like numbers and should be ordered naturally.
Use -m when every input is already sorted and you only need to merge the sorted streams.
Use -u to emit one line for each group of lines with equal sort keys.
gotchas: The current locale can change the result. Set LC_ALL=C when you need byte-based traditional ordering.
Field character positions can be surprising when you use key ranges without a separator or the blank-ignoring option.

ss.summary: `ss` investigates Linux sockets and prints socket statistics. It can show connections, listeners, owning processes, TCP details, timers, summaries, and filtered results.

ss.returns: The command prints socket information or summary statistics to standard output. With `-K`, it attempts to close supported IPv4 and IPv6 sockets.

interview.question: What is `ss` used for?
interview.answer: `ss` investigates sockets and displays socket statistics. It can show more TCP and state information than many other tools.
interview.followUp: How can you reduce name-resolution delays? Use `-n` or `--numeric`, which avoids resolving service names.

interview.question: How do you list listening sockets?
interview.answer: Use `-l` for listening sockets and `-a` for both listening and non-listening sockets. Listening sockets are omitted by default.
interview.followUp: How would you show only TCP listening sockets? Use `ss -t -l`.

interview.question: How does filtering work?
interview.answer: A state filter selects socket states such as `established`, `time-wait`, or `listening`. An expression can further match addresses, ports, devices, marks, or cgroups.
interview.followUp: How can several conditions be combined? Use `and`, `or`, or `not`; adjacent predicates imply `and`.

It provides a modern alternative for many `netstat` socket checks.
Use `-p` to show processes that use the sockets.
Use `-i` to display internal TCP fields such as congestion and round-trip data.
Use `-s` for summary statistics without parsing a full socket list.
Use `-o` to show socket timer details.

The force-close option does not support every socket family.

ssh.explanation: ssh connects to a destination and logs in after the user proves their identity. If a command is supplied, ssh runs it on the remote host instead of starting a login shell. The connection provides encrypted communication and can also carry forwarded X11 connections, TCP ports, and Unix-domain sockets.

interview.question: What does ssh do?
interview.answer: ssh is a remote login client. It connects to a destination, authenticates the user, and can either start a login shell or run a supplied command on the remote host.
interview.followUp: How can it carry other traffic? It can forward X11 connections, arbitrary TCP ports, and Unix-domain sockets through the secure channel.

interview.question: How do you run a remote command?
interview.answer: Use ssh user@host to select both the remote user and host. Add a command after the destination to execute that command remotely instead of opening a login shell.
interview.followUp: How do you select a non-default port? Use -p port, or configure the port per host in the SSH configuration file.

interview.question: How does ssh select a key?
interview.answer: The -i option selects a private-key identity file for public-key authentication. Multiple -i options are allowed, and ssh also tries default identity filenames when applicable.
interview.followUp: What can an agent do? ssh can use identities held by ssh-agent through its environment variables, and AddKeysToAgent can add keys according to configuration.

keyPoints: The destination can use user@hostname or the URI form ssh://user@hostname:port.
Place a command after the destination to run it remotely.
The -C option compresses session data and forwarded X11, TCP, and Unix-domain traffic.
The -D option creates a local SOCKS4 or SOCKS5 proxy whose traffic travels through SSH.
The -N option is useful when SSH is being used only for port forwarding.
The -J option reaches the final host through one or more jump hosts.
gotchas: The remote host requires authentication. A connection can fail if the selected identity or other authentication method is not accepted.
The default escape character is ~, but it works only at the start of a line in sessions with a pseudo-terminal.
Use -C mainly for slow links. Compression can reduce performance on a fast network.

sudo.summary: sudo lets a permitted user run a command as root or another user. A security policy decides what is allowed and whether authentication is required.
sudo.explanation: sudo checks its security policy before running a command with another user's privileges. The default policy is configured through /etc/sudoers or LDAP, and it may require authentication. Policy and I/O plugins can also log attempts and command input or output.

interview.question: What does sudo do?
interview.answer: sudo lets a permitted user run a command as root or another user. A security policy decides whether the command is allowed and whether authentication is needed.
interview.followUp: What is the default policy? The sudoers policy, configured in /etc/sudoers or through LDAP.

interview.question: How do you choose the user and group?
interview.answer: The -u option selects the target user. The -g option selects the target primary group, when the policy permits it.
interview.followUp: How can you inspect permissions first? Use sudo -l to list the invoking user's privileges.

interview.question: How does sudoedit work?
interview.answer: sudoedit edits temporary copies owned by the invoking user, then copies changed files back. The policy selects the editor using SUDO_EDITOR, VISUAL, and EDITOR, in that order.
interview.followUp: What file restrictions apply? Symbolic links and files in user-writable directories are blocked unless the policy explicitly allows them or the user is root.

keyPoints: sudo runs an allowed command as root or another user.
Policy checks use the invoking user's real user ID.
The usual policy is sudoers, configured in /etc/sudoers or LDAP.
Use -v to refresh cached authentication without running a command.
Use -l to list the current user's allowed privileges.
The sudoedit name acts like sudo -e.
gotchas: Edit /etc/sudoers with visudo so syntax errors are checked.
With -n, sudo cannot ask for a password.

Symbolic links.summary: A symbolic link is a special file that stores another pathname. Linux can follow it to a file or directory, including a target that is missing or on another filesystem.
Symbolic links.explanation: A symbolic link is a special file whose contents are a pathname. When a path is used, Linux usually follows the link until it reaches a non-link object, a missing target, or a detected loop. Links can point to files or directories, cross filesystem boundaries, and point to paths that do not yet exist.
Symbolic links.syntax:
int symlink(const char *target, const char *linkpath);
int symlinkat(const char *target, int newdirfd, const char *linkpath);

parameters.name: target
parameters.description: The pathname stored in the new symbolic link. It is not checked by symlink().

parameters.name: linkpath
parameters.description: The new symbolic-link pathname.

parameters.name: newdirfd
parameters.description: Directory file descriptor used as the base for a relative linkpath in symlinkat().

Symbolic links.returns: symlink() and symlinkat() return 0 on success. On error, they return -1 and set errno.

useCases.scenario: Point to a file or directory in another filesystem.

useCases.title: Deferred targets

interview.question: What is a symbolic link?
interview.answer: A symbolic link is a special file that stores a pathname. Linux follows that pathname when resolving a path, while operations such as readlink(), lstat(), unlink(), and rename() can operate on the link itself.
interview.followUp: How does this differ from a hard link? A hard link refers to the same inode as the original name; a symbolic link refers to another pathname and can cross filesystems or point to a directory.

interview.question: What does symlink() do and what does it return?
interview.answer: symlink() creates linkpath with target stored as its contents. It does not check whether target exists, and it returns zero on success or -1 with errno set on failure.
interview.followUp: What happens if linkpath already exists? The call fails rather than overwriting that directory entry.

interview.question: Which system calls operate on the link instead of its target?
interview.answer: For a pathname passed to most system calls, links in dirname components are followed. Most calls also follow a link in the final component, but lstat(), readlink(), unlink(), rename(), and several related calls act on the link itself.
interview.followUp: How can a caller create a link relative to an opened directory? symlinkat() interprets a relative linkpath relative to newdirfd, or relative to the current directory when newdirfd is AT_FDCWD.

keyPoints: The link stores a pathname, not a direct reference to the target's inode.
Unlike hard links, symbolic links can point to directories and targets on another filesystem.
A link can be created before its target; a missing target makes it dangling.
Links in parent-directory parts of a path are normally resolved during system calls.
Calls such as lstat(), readlink(), rename(), and unlink() work on the final link itself.
Recursive file-tree commands normally use a physical walk and do not enter directories through links.
gotchas: Creating a link does not replace an existing directory entry at the link path.
Removing the target name removes the target file, not just the link; the target may still exist through another hard link.
A relative target is resolved from the link's directory, so moving the link can make the target unreachable.

systemctl.summary: `systemctl soft-reboot` restarts systemd userspace without rebooting the kernel. It can switch to a new root at `/run/nextroot/` before restarting userspace.
systemctl.explanation: `systemctl soft-reboot` asks systemd to restart userspace without rebooting the kernel. The command uses `soft-reboot.target`, which starts `systemd-soft-reboot.service`. That service stops remaining processes, optionally changes to `/run/nextroot/`, and starts a new systemd boot transaction.

interview.question: What does a systemd soft reboot do?
interview.answer: A soft reboot restarts userspace while leaving the kernel running. It terminates remaining processes with `SIGTERM`, then uses `SIGKILL`, and starts a new systemd boot transaction.
interview.followUp: What happens if `/run/nextroot/` exists? systemd changes the filesystem root to that location before reexecuting the service manager.

interview.question: How should an application request a soft reboot?
interview.answer: Use `systemctl soft-reboot`. The documentation says applications should not start the target or service directly.
interview.followUp: Why use the command instead? It invokes the supported systemd control path rather than directly executing an internal unit.

interview.question: What are two limitations of a soft reboot?
interview.answer: A soft reboot does not execute `systemd-shutdown`, so programs in `/usr/lib/systemd/system-shutdown/` are skipped. Units that pin host filesystem resources can also keep the old filesystem mounted.
interview.followUp: How can a new userspace root be selected? Place it at `/run/nextroot/`; the soft reboot switches to it before restarting systemd.

keyPoints: The operation restarts userspace but does not reboot the kernel.
Remaining processes first receive `SIGTERM`; systemd then follows with `SIGKILL`.
A directory, mount point, or symlink at `/run/nextroot/` can become the next filesystem root.
After the optional root change, systemd reexecutes the service manager.
The restarted manager creates a new boot transaction similar to a normal reboot.
The supported user-facing command for this operation is `systemctl soft-reboot`.
gotchas: Do not start `soft-reboot.target` or `systemd-soft-reboot.service` directly. Use `systemctl soft-reboot` instead.
Shutdown programs in `/usr/lib/systemd/system-shutdown/` do not run during a soft reboot.
A host filesystem can stay mounted if a running unit pins it with settings such as `BindPaths=`.

systemd units.summary: A systemd unit is a configuration object managed by systemd. Units represent resources or actions such as services, sockets, mounts, targets, timers, and scopes.
systemd units.explanation: A systemd unit is a configuration object that describes a resource or action managed by systemd. Unit types include services, sockets, devices, mounts, targets, paths, timers, slices, and scopes; systemd reads unit files from defined search paths and uses dependencies to build a transaction before running jobs.

systemctl start ssh.service

interview.question: What is a systemd unit?
interview.answer: A unit is a systemd-managed configuration object. Common types include service, socket, mount, target, timer, slice, and scope units.
interview.followUp: How does systemd prepare a start request? It adds the requested unit and dependencies to a transaction, checks ordering for cycles, and then queues the consistent transaction.

interview.question: How does systemd process unit dependencies?
interview.answer: When systemd receives a start or stop request, it creates a temporary transaction containing the requested unit and its dependencies. It checks the transaction and may remove non-essential jobs if needed.
interview.followUp: What can cause the transaction to fail? An unresolvable cycle or conflicting queued jobs can prevent it from being accepted.

interview.question: Where does systemd find unit files?
interview.answer: System units and user units use different search paths. System unit files include locations such as /etc/systemd/system and /usr/lib/systemd/system, while user units use paths under the user's configuration and runtime directories.
interview.followUp: Why can generated units appear? systemd can create units dynamically during boot or when the manager reloads configuration.

keyPoints: systemd manages the system and its services on Linux.
A separate user manager can run services for each logged-in user.
systemd uses control groups to track the processes belonging to units.
Before execution, systemd checks that the requested transaction is consistent.
The dependency ordering must not contain cycles.
Some units can be generated during boot or after a manager reload.
gotchas: Some special units have built-in meaning and must keep their names.
Requesting an operation can create dependency jobs even when the target unit is already active.

tail.explanation: `tail` prints the end of files. By default, it prints 10 lines. It can instead select a byte or line count, read standard input, or keep printing data added to a file.

interview.question: What does `tail` do by default?
interview.answer: `tail` writes the last 10 lines of each file by default. With no file, or with `-`, it reads standard input.
interview.followUp: How do you print the last 100 bytes instead? Use `tail -c 100 file` and note that this counts bytes, not lines.

interview.question: How can you choose the starting part of the output?
interview.answer: Use `-n NUM` or `--lines=NUM` to print the last `NUM` lines. A value beginning with `+` starts at that line instead, skipping the preceding lines.
interview.followUp: What does `tail -n +5 file` output? It outputs from line 5 through the end.

interview.question: How does follow mode work?
interview.answer: `-f` prints data appended to a file as it grows. Its default mode follows the file descriptor; `--follow=name` follows the named file, which is useful when logs are renamed or recreated.
interview.followUp: How can you stop following when a process exits? Add `--pid=PID`; `tail` exits after that process no longer exists.

keyPoints: Without a line or byte option, `tail` prints the final 10 lines of each input file.
If no file is named, or the file name is `-`, input comes from standard input.
`-c NUM` selects bytes from the end. `-c +NUM` starts at the given byte position.
`-n NUM` selects lines from the end. `-n +NUM` starts at line `NUM`.
`-s N` controls the approximate delay between checks while following a file. The default delay is one second.
`-z` treats a NUL character as the line separator instead of a newline.
gotchas: The default `-f` mode follows the open file. If the file is renamed, `tail` keeps following that same file. Use `--follow=name` when the file name should be tracked after rotation.
Several input files cause file-name headers in the output. Use `-q` to suppress them or `-v` to always show them.
Using `-f` without a value follows the file descriptor. It does not follow the file name.
